The ATLAS findings are comparable to those from the CMS, ALICE and LHCb collaborations, with some variation in the peak's apparent magnitude due to differences in detection systems and data analysis approaches. In this study, we investigated the performance-degrading issue of decision-feedback equalizers (DFE) that arises due to burst error propagation in fiber-optic transmissions. Through both theoretical calculations and real-world trial data analysis, we demonstrated that DFE's error propagation causes consecutive binary digits (bits) to be inaccurately corrected, resulting in up to 10^1 consecutive bit errors. Our research also uncovered the relationships between DFE performance decline and several key factors, including the DFE's tap spacing, 7% to 60%, and the number of error propagation bits, directly proportional to tap spacing. Furthermore, we discovered that fiber-optic transmissions' error propagation can be minimized by increasing the DFE's sampling rate, which counterintuitively does not invite further discussion on this topic. Instead, we concentrate on presenting viable alternative modulation techniques and signal processing methods that can surpass the existing 10 Gbit/s capacity limit. Two such strategies were successfully tested and validated during a sea-based field trial. The trial involved transmitting 10 Gbit/s optical signals over 80 km and 40 km spans of Gulf of Aden sea cables, respectively, with the former using the (64QAM) technique and the latter using the (16QAM) technique. The results showed that 10 Gbit/s data transmission can be achieved with a 7% to 10% increase in roll-off factors and a 5 dB power penalty, or using the (16QAM) technique with a 3 dB power penalty. The study's findings also suggest that DFE's error propagation can be contained with a 2 dB power penalty by employing the (256QAM) technique with a 256KHz roll-off factor. However, this approach may not offer the most efficient solution. Ultimately, our research recommends utilizing forward error correction (FEC) codes with a 2 dB power penalty as the simplest and most effective means of mitigating DFE's error propagation. This approach can enable the transmission of 10 Gbit/s data over 80 km of fiber-optic cable. Deep neural network models, such as Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), are frequently used in time series forecasting due to their ability to extract features from sequential data. TCNs utilize a caching mechanism to efficiently process continuous time series data by leveraging convolutional operations. However, when implemented using linear interpolation, these networks can produce inconsistent results if the input sequences do not align with the sampling rate. This issue is particularly pronounced in datasets with irregular time stamps. To address this challenge, a common technique involves interpolating data to a uniform time base before inputting it into the network. Although this approach enhances forecasting accuracy, it increases computational costs and complicates deployment on specialized hardware. This paper introduces a novel trimming technique, where redundant data points are removed without interpolation, until a consistent sampling rate is achieved. We demonstrate that this approach yields comparable performance with minimal computational overhead when compared to the widely used uniform resampling method. Furthermore, our method enables TCNs to be trimmed before being deployed on specialized hardware, such as TPUv3. Our evaluation showcases the efficacy of this approach across multiple time series forecasting benchmarks. For instance, our method surpasses the baseline in the M4 dataset by a significant 11.5% in MAE. This technique also facilitates a 1.5 times performance boost on the TPUv3 when forecasting 100 time series. Our optimized TCN model also exhibits a 24% improvement in real-world application scenarios. The source code for our trimming technique has been made available on the GitHub platform. This optimization strategy can be integrated with other techniques to further enhance forecasting accuracy. This method enables the deployment of TCNs on specialized hardware by reducing the computational overhead by half. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel 3D object representation that
replicates the functionality of Point Clouds and Shapes, but with improved rotational
invariance properties. This representation uses a neural network to predict a set of
feature points and corresponding normals on an object, transforming raw 3D data
into a compact and easily processable form. We demonstrate that NDFs can be
trained through a process called self-supervised feature learning, where the
prediction of feature points and normals is matched against actual data, with the
aim of optimizing a 3D rotation invariant loss function. This allows NDFs to
capture the intrinsic characteristics of an object, with minimal reliance on visual
stimuli. We show that these descriptors can be used in a variety of object
manipulation tasks, including grasping, by utilizing a separate neural network
that predicts possible object poses based on feature points and normals, with the
goal of maximizing a predefined metric such as the distance between points. We
compare NDFs to other 3D object representations, revealing that they excel in
tasks requiring both rotational invariance and accuracy, with the added benefit
of requiring fewer training stimuli. Furthermore, we highlight that these
representations can also be used in a variety of other computer vision tasks,
such as semantic scene segmentation, with minimal modifications. Finally, we
explore the possibility of extending NDFs to other computer vision applications,
such as action recognition, with the integration of additional sensory data. 
We provide comprehensive evidence supporting the rotational invariance of NDFs,
as well as their application in a range of object manipulation and recognition
tasks, with the aim of inspiring further research into the development of 3D
object representations with enhanced invariance properties. Code available at:

We employed the APOGEE-2 spectroscopic survey to investigate the red giant binary star Ton 2 in the Milky Way's bulge, which was previously identified as a binary by Goullaud and Paturel (1971) with an estimated period of roughly 3.24 days. Analyzing the APOGEE-2 spectra with the aid of spectroscopic tomography, we successfully extracted velocity shifts associated with the binary star's motion as a function of wavelength, allowing us to reconstruct its orbital velocity curve. To overcome this issue, using a database of pre-labeled object images has become an effective approach. However, the number of possible solutions grows exponentially with the number of rotation angles, making pose estimation a complex problem. Existing studies typically assume that a 3D object's has a predefined flat surface for projection, known as the ground truth, which significantly reduces the number of possible solutions. Unfortunately, this approach fails when the ground truth is unknown. To tackle this problem, this paper introduces a novel network called DeepHMap++, an enhanced version of the previously proposed DeepHMap, for estimating a 3D object's pose from a single RGB image when the object's 3D mesh map is unknown. Unlike previous studies, this paper focuses on objects with irregular surfaces and unknown 3D mesh maps. To solve this problem, DeepHMap++ combines projection grouping and correspondence learning. First, a projection grouping module identifies the most accurate 2D-3D correspondences by projecting the 3D mesh map onto the image and weighting them based on their consistency. Then, a correspondence learning module uses these high-quality correspondences to estimate the object's pose through optimization. This triplet is found to be an isospin triplet of an $SU(3)$ global symmetry present in the effective theory. We further show that an infinite series of Calabi-Yau three-fold Hodge numbers can be consistently incorporated into the effective theory without violating the triplet's integrity. A general formula is also derived to compute the triplet's mass matrix at an arbitrary point within the complex structure moduli space. This is achieved by formulating a set of constraints that ensure the consistency of the low-energy effective theory, and by establishing a relationship between the triplet's effective interactions and a specific combination of higher derivative interactions that include the graviphoton's self-interactions and a $\theta$-term. A code named 'HodgeTriples' is made available for calculating the mass matrix's eigenvalues at any point within the complex structure moduli space for an arbitrary Calabi-Yau three-fold. A subset of quantum gravity deformed operators, including a $\alpha'^3$ corrected $\theta$-term, can also be obtained from this code. A thorough analysis of the triplet's mass matrix is presented, along with an examination of its low-energy behaviour, and a discussion on the implications of our findings for the consistency of Type IIB string theory in the presence of a non-toric Hodge diagram. A connection between the triplet's integrity and the presence of an $SU(3)$ global symmetry is also highlighted, as well as the potential for this symmetry to be broken at high-energy scales, and a discussion on the triplet's potential for providing a link between Calabi-Yau three-fold Hodge numbers and the low-energy effective theory's parameters. In situations where physical security measures are inadequate or compromised, hardware-based countermeasures that utilize previously inaccessible code become essential for protecting sensitive information, such as cryptographic keys. This work focuses on generating optimized machine code that minimizes trust in hardware components, including physically isolated hardware like secure enclaves and side-channel noise, allowing a malicious OS to guess only a limited amount of information about the code's behavior. By leveraging hardware features like page tables, breakpoints, and cache, we created various attacks that could infer confidential data and developed a technique to defend against these attacks in the case of x86-64 processors. Our experiments showed that even with a large number of trials, our code trust minimization tool couldn't be fully guessed when using a secure enclave, while similar results were observed for in-memory protection. The tool was able to significantly reduce the amount of confidence a malicious OS had in our sample program, from over 80% to less than 50%. Our code received protection at the cost of around 10% performance degradation. In contrast to other solutions that resolve the issue but require multiple runs and significant overhead, our approach provides efficient relief in real-world scenarios. Our research and the developed solution are applicable across different processors that allow memory virtualization and protection, as well as other isolated hardware components, such as FPGAs and custom hardware components, and our technique could serve as a foundation for side-channel secure programming. Furthermore, our technique could be used to tackle other confidentiality-related issues, such as ensuring that only authorized hardware accesses occur and preventing the leakage of sensitive information through side channels, such as cache and branch prediction. Our approach involves two main components: first, we employ linear regression to establish relationships between monomer properties and system variables, but we then use an integer optimization method to select a subset of these connections that are highly predictive and likely to represent actual connections between monomers, thus producing a set of polymers with defined actions; second, we leverage the derived polymers by solving an inference problem to identify the specific combination of monomers that can perform a particular task, such as deblurring images. By applying our framework to a common image dataset, we demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional deblurring techniques. Additionally, we explore ways to enhance our approach by incorporating additional information about the monomers and the task at hand. Our code is now publicly available on GitHub under the MIT License. We explore various aspects of our framework and provide supporting evidence for our research on the monomer prediction forum. Furthermore, we present our results at the ICLR 2021 workshop on Inverse Problems, Optimization, and Statistics. Optimal control techniques can be used to enhance the performance of interconnected nonlinear systems whose dynamics are subject to tight interconnection constraints. However, the difficulty lies in obtaining an interconnection matrix that accurately reflects the degree of interconnection between the systems. In this paper, we focus on a dual-patient breathing model, aiming to apply optimal control to promote synchronized breathing rates without revealing the individual inhaled volumes, as required during the COVID-19 pandemic. By leveraging direct transcription and a specific collocation method, we successfully transformed the optimal control problem into a boundary-value problem, thus circumventing the challenge of the interconnection matrix. Furthermore, the paper concludes with a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical breathing rates and numerical simulations of the dual-patient breathing model under various delay conditions. These optimal control techniques and the model are also applicable to other dual-patient scenarios, as demonstrated through simulation. The code used in this paper is publicly available on GitHub. The boundary-value problem approach offers a feasible path for controlling interconnected nonlinear systems across various industries and fields. The paper is targeted at academics and industrial professionals working with optimal control and interconnected nonlinear systems. Detecting esophageal cancer in its early stages is crucial, and developing reliable computer algorithms for identifying the disease from CT scans is essential for this purpose. Presently, medical professionals rely on visual inspections of these scans to determine if a tumor is present. However, this method has its limitations as it can be time-consuming and may lead to errors if the tumor is small or located deep within the esophagus. To enhance accuracy and efficiency, an automated system has been proposed that uses computer deep learning to identify and outline neoplasms in CT images of the esophagus. One such model, the dense dense unet model, was particularly effective in this task due to its use of dense blocks that efficiently extract and utilize the information from different parts of the image, thereby minimizing the need for external multi-scale fusion components. Moreover, the proposed model's dense attention mechanism enables the targeted collection of contextual information from different dense block levels, thereby optimizing feature extraction and segmentation performance. When tested and validated using a dataset of 240 CT images, the model demonstrated exceptional precision and reliability, with an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.9232 indicating a high degree of accuracy in neoplasm segmentation. The model's efficiency was also measured, with each prediction taking no more than 30 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-world clinical applications. The proposed model outperformed existing competitors due to its innovative dense attention and dense block design, and you can access its source code through a publicly available GitHub repository. When applied to actual clinical settings, the model demonstrated a high level of safety and efficiency, with no instances of tumor misclassification. Overall, this model represents a significant advancement in esophageal neoplasm segmentation, with a high degree of accuracy and a short processing time that is comparable to human professionals. The model's performance was consistent across a wide range of neoplasm types, with an average score of 0.9232 on the test dataset, and it is now being explored for use in actual clinical environments due to its high safety and efficiency levels. The model's innovative design, which incorporates a dense attention mechanism and dense blocks, has enabled it to extract and utilize contextual information from different parts of an image, thereby optimizing feature extraction and segmentation performance. The model's performance was evaluated on a large dataset of 240 CT images, and it demonstrated a high degree of accuracy, with an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.9232, and a short processing time of 30 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-world clinical applications.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a key extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve and analyze text-based information. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies leverage sequential neural network models, which do not adequately capture the rich information within entities, nor do they accurately determine entity relationships. This work reconsiders the entity-based structure and proposes a novel, holistic parsing approach for nested NER, incorporating a specialized graph structure that captures entity properties and relationships. A corresponding holistic model is also introduced, which incorporates a nested grid representation that incorporates information about the entities' types and previous entities encountered during the parsing process. This holistic model outperforms sequential models on various nested NER datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of a unified structure in accurately identifying entities. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the extraction of multiple entity types from a single passage, as demonstrated across different languages and datasets. Research into the localization of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks has generated significant interest in recent years. This study focuses on the precise location of mobile nodes in networks that are subject to interference from other technologies. It identifies the source of ambiguity in existing research as resulting location estimates being expressed in terms of the network's grid size, rather than a more practical unit such as meters. To address this issue, the paper develops novel algorithms for location estimation in two scenarios: first, when the mobile node and reference nodes use the same technology, and second, when they use different technologies. It also explores ways to determine the maximum achievable precision, either by assuming a perfect understanding of interference, or in cases where only the network's density is known. Ultimately, the work shows that location estimates can be highly inaccurate, often far exceeding the network's grid size. As such, the paper suggests that the term "range-free" localization is misleading, as it implies costs associated with obtaining reference node locations. Two potential solutions to increase precision are also examined, including the development of more robust algorithms, and using nodes located at the edge of a network's coverage as reference points for future localizations. Overall, the work highlights the need for a more precise evaluation of localization algorithms, as well as the development of secure and robust coding methods, especially in applications where location information has critical implications. Finally, the paper is also relevant to the broader field of wireless communication research, as it is underpinned by the same fundamental principles and concepts. Consequently, its findings and outcomes are equally applicable to this field. This work is an extended version of an earlier paper that was presented at the IEEE GLOBECOM 2018 conference. Human-generated descriptions are utilized to train and evaluate automatic image description methods, however their accuracy is frequently compromised due to the subjectivity of human producers and the diverse nature of description formats. Moreover, the vast majority of these descriptions are written with the intent of being used as multiple-choice selection options, rather than a standalone description of the image. In contrast to relying solely on these descriptions, our proposed approach makes use of a diverse reference dataset that is created by a large group of humans and serves as a standard for evaluating the accuracy of automatic image descriptions. In particular, our dataset, which is comprised of 100,000 descriptions, is utilized to investigate the disparity between human-generated descriptions that are produced through various methods, such as multiple-choice selection, unrestricted text entry, and description of the image's central focus, as well as the average level of these descriptions' accuracy. In addition, our approach incorporates several automated image description assessment methods that are based on different metrics, including accuracy, natural language, and diversity. In the context of the Flickr30k dataset, our research demonstrates that using a diverse reference dataset that is created by a large group of humans that represents the average level of automatic image descriptions' accuracy serves as a more reliable performance indicator than the descriptions that are produced through multiple-choice selection alone. Moreover, our research highlights the importance of selecting description generation methods that are representative of actual human-produced descriptions, as well as the need to consider the diversity of these descriptions in order to obtain an accurate assessment of automatic image descriptions. In addition, our research demonstrates that several existing automated image description assessment methods are either inaccurate or incomplete, and therefore they should be reevaluated and potentially revised in order to better reflect the average level of actual human-produced descriptions. Tantalum oxide Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a significant material with numerous applications, yet contrary to expectations, Ta$_2$O$_3$ xeroxes typically yield a Ta$_2$O$_5$ solid with an unclear crystal structure.  We employed experimental techniques, including x-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy in combination with theoretical simulations to investigate the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure obtained from reducing Ta$_2$O$_3$ in air.  Our experimental findings suggest a Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure comprising two TaO$_3$ layers connected by a single oxygen atom, which we verified through Monte Carlo simulations under conditions mimicking the oxidation process.  This Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure is analogous to the layer TaOx morphology found in studies of TaOx reduction, particularly for x=3.  Our calculations using first-principles methods show that this Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure has a stable energy state, and it exhibits electronic properties suitable for display applications.  We further demonstrate that this Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure can be achieved through the annealing of thin Ta$_2$O$_5$ films, and our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the physics governing the TaOx system.  We also explore the possibility of growing this Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure through low-temperature molecular beam deposition, supported by simulations of the structural evolution of Ta$_2$O$_5$ films as a function of substrate temperature.  Our research provides valuable insights for tailoring the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ through different synthesis pathways.  We further examine the potential of this Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure in nanotechnology, including its surface energy characteristics, and the results indicate that this structure may yield TaOx nanocrystals with sizes above 2 nm.  Our findings are also relevant to identifying the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers in p-channel TaOx field-effect transistors, and we suggest that these devices may operate at temperatures above 100 K.  Our research offers a framework for investigating the physics underlying other transition metal oxides.  We demonstrate that this Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure can be achieved through the annealing of thin Ta$_2$O$_5$ films, and our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the physics governing the TaOx system.

Previous studies attributed the dissemination of misinformation to be fueled by the "Big Sort," a phenomenon where like-minded individuals are geographically isolated into separate communities. However, researchers argue that this theory has been misapplied and instead suggest that it is the "Big Geographic Sort" – a process of self-segregation within those communities – that drives the spread of misinformation. Using Reddit data, the study reveals that users who engage in the dissemination of misinformation are more likely to be isolated within their own social networks. Furthermore, it shows that users who are more prone to spreading misinformation are often those who are more likely to share content from news sources, as well as those with lower educational attainment and those who are more politically active. The study demonstrates that the "Big Geographic Sort" occurs when users with these characteristics share information that is later amplified by influencers. As a result, users who are more likely to spread misinformation are those who are more socially connected to those who are more isolated within their community, but still hold extreme views. The study's findings suggest that mitigating the dissemination of misinformation requires a deeper understanding of the complex social dynamics at play, specifically those involving self-segregation within communities, as well as the development of community-specific fact-checking strategies. The study's methodology relies on a combination of natural language processing, machine learning, and network analysis to gather and analyze data from Reddit users. The study's findings on the role of education and political engagement in the dissemination of misinformation are consistent with previous research, while the study's findings on the function of the "Big Geographic Sort" contribute to an ongoing debate in the field. The study's results demonstrate the significance of the "Big Geographic Sort" in the dissemination of misinformation, while also highlighting the importance of community structure in the spread of information. The study's findings can be applied to the broader context of the dissemination of misinformation, as well as the importance of considering community structure in network analysis. Teaching and guiding others through different tasks with the aid of demonstration has been a widely used method by humans to assist robots in understanding task objectives. It has been observed that humans employ auditory feedback to supplement their demonstrations, offering a complementary means of communication. Nonetheless, the intricate language used by humans in such situations remains poorly understood, hindering the development of robust vision-based learning methods. This study aims to illuminate the auditory aspect of demonstrations by analyzing speech used by human instructors as they demonstrate various tasks to a robot, across multiple frequencies and several core aspects of task demonstrations. Our findings, derived from 12 diverse task sets and 30 human instructors, reveal the prevalence of descriptive language, pointing out key aspects of the task, along with any restrictions or adjustments required. Our research also delves into the variations in speech patterns based on the underlying structure of the tasks, the instructions given, and the skills already possessed by the robot. Our results provide valuable insights that can inform the design of learning methods, helping them to effectively utilize both visual and auditory feedback to facilitate more efficient and accurate robot learning. This research is an initial exploration, and further study is needed to fully comprehend the complex language used by humans during demonstrations. Nonetheless, the results presented here can already provide insights for improving the learning method, leading to a more robust and precise robot training. Utilizing astrometry data from the most recent celestial observations, we evaluate the impact of Planet X on the positioning and movement of the known planets across the sky. Our analysis indicates that a massive Planet X with an orbit within the Kuiper Belt could be identified by its gravitational effect on the positioning of Neptune, and that such a discovery could potentially be made with existing technology. However, if the Planet X lies outside the Kuiper Belt, its gravitational effect would be masked by the scattering of objects within the belt, and it would be more difficult to identify by this method. Deep neural network-based machine translation models have achieved remarkable success in various language pairs, however, their interpretation remains unclear. Recent studies suggest that neural machine translation can be viewed as rewriting source text into the target language, but the underlying structural changes are not well grasped. In order to enhance the interpretability of neural machine translation, the paper proposes utilizing a monolingual translation archive, which involves training a neural machine translation model and then leveraging its output to create a target-language corpus connected to the original source texts. By doing so, a neural machine translation model can be reinterpreted as a neural language model that generates target-language sentences corresponding to the source texts. This reinterpretation provides a clear understanding of how neural machine translation works and offers a method to improve its performance through both source and target-language enhancements. Experiments conducted on multiple language pairs demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving neural machine translation accuracy. Furthermore, this archive's utility is shown across multiple machine translation tasks, including abstractive summarization and neural machine translation with multiple sources. The proposed method's effectiveness is observed across various language pairs, including English-German, English-French, and English-Chinese. The code and models devised in this research are made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NeuralMachineInterpretation. The paper's findings are also illustrated through a case study on the English-German language pair, and the associated document is available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/NeuralMachineInterpretation/blob/main/CaseStudy_EnglishGerman.pdf. The proposed monolingual translation archive's potential benefits and potential challenges are discussed in the paper's conclusion. The paper's final section presents future research directions centered on the monolingual translation archive, including ways to integrate existing machine translation models without starting from scratch, diverse sentence types in machine translation, and the extension of this work to low-resource language scenarios. The paper's ideas on future research are also accompanied by a corresponding roadmap available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/NeuralMachineInterpretation/blob/main/FutureResearchDirections.pdf. The paper's conclusions are summarized in its last section, and a set of key terms are defined in the paper's glossary available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/NeuralMachineInterpretation/blob/main/Glossary.pdf. Our dataset comprises 15,000 images, drawn from three sources, spanning various MRI sequences, modulation schemes, and pathology conditions.  To generalize across multiple factors, we employ a ensemble of models, thereby minimizing overfitting. Moreover, our approach proves versatile in accommodating various machine learning models, as seen in our comparative analysis of nine different models. To address this challenge, we propose an agent-based optimization method that considers privately owned electric cars as flexible agents, capable of both driving and charging on the urban network. Our goal is to maximize the minimum of 30-minute distribution times for all nodes within a defined area by leveraging the flexibility of these agents. We utilize a multi-agent version of the 2-path route choice model and an electric car demand model that takes into account factors such as charging cost, driving distance, and network congestion. To improve solution efficiency, we apply a hybrid method combining the Multi-agent Electric Car Distribution Optimization algorithm with the Neighborhood Search method, yielding optimal or near-optimal results for small networks. For larger urban networks, we present a method for estimating high-quality solutions. Simulation results using real-world urban networks indicate that our proposed algorithm can generate superior solutions to existing methods, and we provide strategic recommendations for optimizing private electric car deployment to maximize the effectiveness of our algorithm. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the value of integrating private electric cars into urban distribution network planning, leading to increased network resilience and flexibility. Furthermore, we explore the concept of crowdsourcing car flexibility through shared ownership and operation, and examine the associated challenges and potential solutions, including but not limited to monetary incentives, charging infrastructure placement, and network security. Lastly, we discuss several pathways for further research in this emerging field. In conclusion, as the number of privately owned electric cars continues to rise, their impact on urban distribution networks will only intensify, making it essential to develop more adaptable and resilient distribution systems that leverage the benefits of these vehicles. Ultimately, this will in turn create new opportunities for shared electric car ownership and usage, as well as contribute to the overall sustainability of our transportation infrastructure. However, its proof relies on a lemmas that is specific to the tree-structured diagrams associated with finite Coxeter groups, including those of type A (linear), B (orthogonal), and W (symmetric). The vast majority of Type Ia Supernovae are used to measure the current cosmological model due to their reliable luminosity, despite being affected by weak gravitational lensing. Gravitational lensing distorts light from these events, influencing their observed brightness and redshift. Using the Pantheon SNIA database, our analysis accounts for intrinsic color and shape distortions to measure the lensing impact. As a result, we find that the standard cosmological model remains accurate, with weak gravitational lensing explaining approximately 0.008 of the relative uncertainty in SNIA data. This research's limited lensing effect on such events is significant, as it improves the accuracy of future observations under similar lensing conditions. Furthermore, we anticipate a more substantial lensing impact in future SNIA surveys with significantly greater data sets. To minimize the lensing effect's influence, future low-resolution observations are recommended for only the brightest Type Ia Supernovae. Leveraging future multi-object spectrographs like MASSIV or future SNIA surveys with similar lensing magnification limits could reduce the impact of weak gravitational lensing to a fraction of its current influence. Lastly, as such events serve as crucial cosmological tools, it is essential to be aware of the influence of weak gravitational lensing when interpreting their data. Furthermore, this research highlights the significance of distinguishing between the effects of weak gravitational lensing and other SNIA biases, particularly in the fourth generation of such observations. As such observations are primarily light-weighted, we propose using a new lensing-weighted estimator that takes into account the amplification of such events. This new estimator demonstrates a more significant scatter than traditional methods but is just as accurate in predicting the true SNIA density. Lastly, based on this research, future SNIA surveys with similar lensing conditions and magnification limits are expected to be dominated by lensing effects at redshifts greater than 0.07. As such observations are primarily light-weighted, the impact of weak gravitational lensing on such events is feeble but their significance in the broader astrophysical community makes this effect significant. Highly efficient light localization can be achieved in photonic materials through the use of T-shaped hubs within the SOI structure. By cutting silicon islands and creating T-shaped resonators, we investigate how varying the width of these islands, as well as the distance between them, affects the mode field distribution and optical loss in the material. Our research indicates that increasing the width of the silicon islands or the distance between them leads to increased mode field size, but also results in increased optical loss. Our findings can be applied to the design of secure light storage systems, as well as systems utilizing T hubs within the SOI structure. Additionally, we present a method for calculating the mode field size in these systems. Furthermore, we explore potential applications of T hubs in the SOI structure for the sensitive detection of small changes, and demonstrate the ability of these systems to detect changes in air refractive index as small as 10^-4.

The significant challenge of analyzing stellar activity is posed by absorption lines resulting from cool plasmas, which can mask other features and make it difficult to retrieve accurate spectral diagnostics. To overcome this issue using least-squares deconvolution, our research compares three different line databases – one based on the solar spectrum in the Solar Spectrum Synthesisization, the other two derived from the UNeeded Lines catalog – to determine the most effective approach to line selection for a variety of elements. Our findings indicate that using a large number of lines does not necessarily yield the most accurate deconvolution results; instead, we should focus on selecting lines that are sensitive to specific elements, taking into account the effects of blending, using a large number of lines only for hydrogen, and that random line selection can produce equivalent results using a significantly smaller number of lines, thus significantly reducing the computational time. Notably, we discovered that the main factor influencing the performance of line selection is not the specific line list but rather the selection of lines that are sensitive to the particular element of interest. Our study provides a starting point for optimizing the UNeeded Lines catalog for the purpose of analyzing stellar spectra using least-squares deconvolution. Our analysis is complemented by synthetic spectra that demonstrate the advantages of this approach over traditional methods. Our research is relevant to the broad range of spectroscopic stellar activity studies, particularly those involving the analysis of spectral lines that provide fundamental information about stellar parameters, such as mass, radius, surface temperature, and rotational velocity. Our study is also significant in the context of the ongoing and future high-resolution stellar spectrography missions that will employ least-squares deconvolution to analyze stellar spectra, including the Shrimp, ESPaDIN, and MEGES instruments aboard the ESPA, as well as the ESPaDIN and IRDAS instruments aboard the ESPA. Deep neural network-based object classifiers are often used in critical applications despite being trained on diverse, unlabelled images from the internet. Consequently, it is crucial to understand the contextual framework in which these classifiers operate, as their performance can be influenced by various elements of the scene. This paper introduces a comprehensive contextual assessment for such classifiers, encompassing six interrelated aspects of the scene that contribute to context. We differentiate between high-level scene settings and low-level visual details that comprise context. We develop a unified, end-to-end framework that incorporates both setting and detail information to generate a context score for each object class. This framework serves as a universal evaluator for the contextual framework in which any given object classifier operates. Notably, our proposed approach achieves notable accuracy improvements over baseline classifiers while maintaining exceptional performance on the original task. We exhaustively examine various context aspects and their respective associations with the scene settings and visual details. Our research is complemented by an interactive visualization tool that enables intuitive exploration of our findings in conjunction with our Context Assessment Dataset (CAD) now available for public access. Ultimately, our work highlights the significance of contextual framework assessment in the deployment of pre-trained object classifiers, emphasizing the need to incorporate context-aware approaches in conjunction with selection and tuning strategies. The Ideal Kidney Match problem has long been a subject of interest for mathematicians and computer scientists in its own right, and also as a simplification of complex kidney exchange networks. Originally formulated in 1963, the problem involves determining the largest subset of a given set of kidney pairs that can be paired up for ideal (one-to-one) transplants. In this paper, we explore a variation of this problem where some pairs are incompatible with each other, and we aim to maximize the number of pairs that can be ideally matched. We present a new variant of this problem that eliminates time limits and other constraints on pair pairing, and we prove that a relaxed version of this variant has a minimum weight subgraph criterion. We also develop efficient algorithms for solving both this relaxed version and a more constrained variant with time limits. Furthermore, we investigate a version of this problem where pairs have different weights and provide a generalization of the minimum weight subgraph criterion for this case. Additionally, we discuss potential applications of these results to the Ideal Kidney Match problem and provide empirical evaluations of our algorithms. In particular, we provide the first ideal exchanges for large instances with time constraints and demonstrate that our algorithms perform well in practice, often approaching optimal solutions quickly. This distinct approach differs from traditional kernel-based methods, which explicitly define the mapping but do not necessarily imply a specific implicit function, thus leveraging the generalization capabilities of INNs. This combination of implicit representations and stochastic optimization techniques yields improved performance and flexibility in modeling complex probability distributions, especially when working with noisy or incomplete data. INNs particularly enable the creation of highly detailed and realistic images, sounds, and videos by providing a systematic way to expand inputs through an implicit kernel, ensuring that generated examples adhere to the training data's statistical characteristics. This overview explores the implicit kernel's effects on learning and data representation, examining how it expands traditional kernel methods by permitting the modeling of intricate relationships and the incorporation of prior knowledge embedded in input variables. As a result, many applications, including classification, regression, and generative tasks, can benefit from the implicit kernel's ability to capture and utilize global and local patterns in data. Furthermore, research on the implicit kernel's connection to traditional kernel methods and its extension to other probabilistic models is also discussed, along with the resulting generalizations and the opportunity to incorporate external information about inputs, which in turn enables the creation of highly accurate models for diverse data sets, such as text, with potential improvements in convergence rate and generalization performance. Recent studies utilizing neural network-based word representations have claimed significant performance improvements in text classification tasks, including sentiment analysis. However, a methodological flaw in previous research has hindered a thorough assessment of these representations' effectiveness, specifically in capturing the polarity intended by the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. To address this limitation, our research introduces two novel assessments to evaluate the quality of these representations. Firstly, we develop a comprehensive semantic space evaluation by combining multiple methods to extensively examine the embedding distributions according to the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. Secondly, we introduce practical applications for various sentiment analysis tasks, leveraging the dictionary as a reference standard. Our results reveal that none of the tested word representations, including neural network-trained embeddings and baselines like Word2Vec and GloVe, satisfactorily capture the intended polarity by comprehensively adhering to the dictionary's definitions in semantic space or achieving consistent classification accuracy in practical applications. Our research offers a more precise assessment of these representations in the context of sentiment analysis and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary. Additionally, we provide all trained models, implementation details, and results to facilitate further exploration and improvement of neural network-based word representations in the domain of finance. Our work also highlights the importance of meticulous evaluation processes to avoid misinterpretation of seemingly positive results and to ensure responsible use of word representations in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we emphasize the value of cross-method evaluation to facilitate comparison and competition among different representation models. Our study sets a precedent for rigorous evaluation of word representations in sentiment analysis and similar text classification tasks. In conclusion, our research underscores the necessity for word representations that not only excel in task performance but also comprehensively capture the underlying semantics and intended polarity as defined by reference standards. In the context of our research, we recommend the use of simple yet robust neural network architectures for word representations that can provide a balance between semantic richness and practical application effectiveness. Ultimately, our work paves the way for the development of more comprehensive evaluation protocols and higher-performance word representations that can effectively capture the complexities and nuances of sentiment and other semantic phenomena. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of open-access data sharing and collaborative evaluation to accelerate breakthroughs in the field. In the interest of advancing research in this area, we openly provide all trained models, implementation details, and results. In the future, we anticipate even more refined word representations that can not only excel in sentiment analysis but also in other text classification tasks, such as topic modeling, and the detection of hate speech, trolls, and fake news. In the realm of formal semantics, our primary goal is to understand how language users convey and gather information from statements, which is closely tied to the fundamental concepts of truth, falsity, and rationality. This study focuses on unary connectives within the system, specifically addressing, asserting, denying, and questioning. By integrating unary connectives into a quantum framework, particularly using the Kleisli category based on the Giry monoid, we aim to provide a novel interpretation for these operators that reflects their functional role in language. This approach results in a diverse range of unary connectives, each with a distinct information transfer effect, spanning from the same as the classical counterparts to significantly more intricate behaviors, such as partial truth or the blending of statements. This research offers a unique framework for exploring the intricate aspects of language, including the interplay between numerous unary connectives and the way they affect information transfer in language. Furthermore, this study paves the way for a broader examination of the language of types, especially when it comes to the properties of distributivity and the behavior of mixtures. This is particularly evident in the case of the quantum model, which raises intriguing questions about the implications of combining statements like "it is true that it is raining" with "it is false that it is raining." This is just a starting point for our investigation into the world of types and the underlying structure of language. Ultimately, this research is an exploration of the language of types with a focus on the fundamental nature of truth, falsity, and rationality in a way that is both theoretically sound and linguistically meaningful. This study is an evolution of the work presented in "A Quantum Semantics for Polarized Modalities" and "A Quantum Semantics for S4 and BPP" within the context of hyperintensional types. We investigate the challenge of learning optimal policies in multiple player games against non-oblivious opponents under best response conditions. Unlike the single player case, where positive results exist, our findings reveal that several important game theory problems encounter insurmountable difficulties when it comes to learning equilibria under uncertainty. Nevertheless, we do uncover a useful subclass of multiplayer games amenable to learning rationalizable equilibria. Moreover, we demonstrate that any game that satisfies specific technical conditions is part of this subclass, thereby providing a theoretically grounded justification for the effectiveness of our approach on games that appear in real-world multiplayer competitions. To address this challenge, we develop a novel learning algorithm based on a novel approach to dealing with uncertainty, and showcase its effectiveness in achieving optimal performance in a variety of multiplayer game scenarios. Our algorithm is simple to execute, robust to model inaccuracies, and exhibits compelling performance when applied to a range of real-world multiagent learning tasks. Interestingly, we also show that any game that fails to meet our theoretical criteria can be modified trivially to produce adverse effects on learning. Our findings provide a valuable contribution to the field of multiagent learning by identifying a crucial insight that can guide the design of efficient learning algorithms. Furthermore, our results are underpinned by a novel extension to a well-known concept in computer science, thereby enhancing our understanding of the complex interplay between learning and strategy interaction. Overall, our work lays the groundwork for a broader exploration of multiagent learning, while also providing practical solutions to a range of challenging multiplayer game theory problems. To further explore this research, the code for our experiments has been made available in an accompanying repository. This work has been presented at the 35th Conference on Learning Theory (COLT 2022) and the 25th International Conference on Artificial Agents (AAMAS 2022). It has also received the Best Student Paper Award at the 25th International Conference on Artificial Agents (AAMAS 2022). Additionally, it has been shortlisted for the Best Student Paper Award at the 35th Conference on Learning Theory (COLT 2022). An investigation is conducted to explore the long-term behavior of disease models that incorporate network rewiring, specifically focusing on systems that exhibit preventive restructuring – i.e., networks break apart to prevent further infection spread. Two dynamic models are examined: an ER graph model that undergoes random edge removal and substitution, and a Lattice model with nearest-neighbor connectivity. In general, preventive restructuring accelerates the epidemic's early phase but eventually slows its spread. However, it also introduces a critical threshold, below which the epidemic's final prevalence is independent of its initial intensity. Interestingly, some underlying network features can remain unaltered even as the structure changes dynamically. By analyzing these features, a more general framework is proposed that provides insight into how preventive restructuring affects the epidemic's temporal evolution. Notably, the accelerated phase is characterized by an exponential decrease in infection spread, until a crossover point where it gives way to a slower power-law decline. The accelerated phase's duration is found to be directly proportional to the average degree of connectivity and the probability of successful vaccination. The models examined also reveal that preventive restructuring can lead to hysteresis in epidemic dynamics, where different trajectories yield distinct equilibrium infection spread outcomes. The study's findings are relevant to the design of vaccination strategies in complex networks that evolve over time. Furthermore, the analysis conducted in this study is also applicable to broader contexts where preventive failure or reduction leads to accelerated change, followed by a more gradual, power-law driven convergence. The mathematical frameworks and theoretical frameworks developed in this study can be adapted to examine other epidemiological models that incorporate network changes, as well as to understand accelerated phenomena in other areas, such as accelerated phase transitions in physical systems, accelerated sedimentation in granular matter, and accelerated fixation in evolutionary systems. A new framework for exponential acceleration in complex systems is proposed, along with a new exponent that captures this phenomenon, and this framework is shown to yield results that are consistent with existing theories. The study also raises fundamental questions about the interplay between local stability and global behavior in complex systems, and the varying roles of randomness, nonlinearity, and degree of connectivity in determining whether a system exhibits local asymptotic stability, unbounded growth, or a mix of both. The study provides a new perspective on the historic vs. real-time behavior debate in complex systems, and it suggests that in some cases, a system's historical data may not accurately predict its future behavior in a real-time scenario. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterized by a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$. Furthermore, we prove that $\lambda$ equals the average of the Ricci operator's trace, thereby confirming the condition for the existence of such solitons. Moreover, we prove that on compact nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a steady Cotton soliton is equal to the negative divergence of the Ricci operator divided by 3, establishing a direct link between $\lambda$ and the Ricci flow. Lastly, we illustrate the incompatibility of a conformal steady Cotton soliton on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Additionally, we provide the transformation of a shrinking Cotton soliton, resulting in a potential vector field that is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field, yielding a conformal steady Cotton soliton. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the potential expansion of previous research on Cotton solitons within nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Furthermore, we establish the connection between a steady Cotton soliton and the Ricci flow, specifically the conformal Laplacian equation. Lastly, we outline the potential exploration into other types of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds.

Although experience replay is a widely adopted method to prevent overlapping experiences from dominating the updates, it suffers from several limitations, notably the inefficient use of training data. We have investigated the metallic phase of LaNiO$_3$ when it is part of a LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattice of five-layer thickness and studied its evolution within a LaAlO$_3$ matrix of varying thickness.  Using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR, we have measured the NMR relaxation rates and found them to indicate a strong correlation between the LaNiO$_3$ metallic phase and the number of LaNiO$_3$ layers.  Additionally, we have found that the LaAlO$_3$ layer thickness has a minimal impact on the NMR measurements at low temperatures, but does affect the LaNiO$_3$ magnetic susceptibility at higher temperatures.  Our results suggest that the LaNiO$_3$ metallic state can be maintained even when the superlattice is isolated, and that the temperature at which the magnetic susceptibility starts to increase with temperature depends on the number of LaNiO$_3$ layers. Effective dialogue systems are crucial for comprehending and generating complex, realistic conversations.
Current evaluation frameworks, such as DSTC, fall short due to their limited scope and simple worldviews, hindrance to the development of advanced dialogue technology.
In response to these limitations, we present MultiTalk, a highly branching and realistic testbed featuring varied conversations.
This dataset comprises 1,001 complex turns across 51 distinct topics, organized into seven categories by human annotators based on world assumptions and then further combined into two comprehensive categories by machine learners using supervised approaches.
We employ multiple evaluation metrics, including single-turn and multi-turn metrics, to assess the performance of state-of-the-art dialogue systems.
Our evaluation reveals significant disparities in performance across different topics and worldviews, underscoring the necessity for diverse evaluation data to ensure the broad applicability of dialogue technology.

In particular, we include the source code for both text-based interaction and demonstration videos. 
In addition, we have presented preliminary findings at the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, and the corresponding paper can be found here https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04451. 
We invite stakeholders in the natural language processing community to join us in exploring this novel evaluation framework and the accompanying MultiTalk dataset. 
We have initiated an associated forum https://github.com/ghrua/MultiTalk/discussions to facilitate discussion and collaboration.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension of the MediaWiki platform, designed to address the limitations of traditional knowledge collaboration tools. Developed by the WorkingWiki Project, this derivative aims to provide a comprehensive framework for exploring complex concepts and developing actionable plans as a team. By incorporating features from effective collaboration methodologies, such as Design Thinking and Co-Design, WorkingWiki features eight specialized pages tailored to facilitate each phase of the collaboration process. These phases are defined by the WorkingWiki Project as Identify, Explore, Analyze, Develop, Refine, Plan, Execute, and Assess stages. To ensure the integrity of research efforts, WorkingWiki introduces a built-in validation process, leveraging a derivative of the Trust Network algorithm to evaluate the credibility of sources. A built-in entity recognition module, inspired by SPARQL, enables the identification of entities and their attributes within wiki pages, facilitating their use in subsequent research phases. WorkingWiki's research pipeline derives from the Entity-Relationship Model and includes an entity recognition step, followed by relationships between entities, their attributes, and associated data. To facilitate the discovery of reliable information, WorkingWiki introduces an iterative scoring system for ranking sources based on their credibility, relevance, and relevance to the underlying entity structure. The project's research framework is complemented by a built-in discussion forum, enabling the exploration of complex concepts through discussion, idea generation using brain dumping, and the development of actionable plans using the What-If Tool. WorkingWiki's execution layer features integrations with popular automation and execution tools, such as GitHub Actions and tmps, for validating in vitro research assumptions and implementing in silico models. The project's assessment module evaluates the outcomes of collective research, relying on an open-source derivative of the SCORE framework that integrates the Trust Network's credibility assessments for each entity and research assumption, along with entity-specific metrics, to produce a cumulative credibility score for the entire research effort. WorkingWiki's executive layer is supported by an open-source leadership framework that promotes the development of a knowledge culture within research teams, fostering a spirit of discovery, a willingness to learn from failures, and a commitment to upholding the project's core values, code of ethics, and scientific standards. The WorkingWiki Project's derivative media wiki is available for public download at https://workingwiki.org/wiki/WorkingWiki_Derivative, along with the WorkingWiki Project's website at https://workingwiki.org/wiki/WorkingWiki_Project, providing access to the project's documentation, source code, and community forum. By applying an external field and varying temperature, we study the dynamics of particle clustering. Our findings reveal that an equilibrium coexistence of clustered and dispersed states occurs at a temperature-dependent threshold, separated by a temperature barrier. This temperature barrier regulates the rate at which particles switch between these two states. Our theoretical analysis focuses particularly on the effects of changing temperature on the clustering process. In contrast to three-dimensional lattice fluids, the temperature threshold and barrier in two-dimensional systems exhibit non-linear relationships with temperature. Additionally, the impact of changing temperature on cluster dynamics in two-dimensional systems differs significantly from that in their three-dimensional counterparts. A notable distinction in cluster kinetics is identified in a two-dimensional system with a strong external field and low temperature, where the rate of transition is dominated by a high-frequency component that is sensitive to temperature changes. The abundance of solar gamma-ray bursts exceeds that of terrestrial gamma-ray bursts, yet the source of gamma-rays in solar flares remains poorly understood. We propose a vector model for detecting ultra-high energy photons, which uses directions of solar magnetic field lines and neutron star magnetic field directions to identify potential directions for gamma-ray detection. By applying this model to historical solar flare data, we found instances of gamma-ray flux above the typical solar flux levels in the directions of magnetic field lines and neutron star magnetic field directions. Notably, the neutron star magnetic field in the Scorpius X-1 system shows the highest gamma-ray flux among all directions, with a statistically significant excess flux of $1.56\pm0.30$ photons cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ in the 10-300 GeV range, exceeding the typical solar flux by a factor of more than ten. We estimate the total gamma-ray energy released in the 3.5 billion cubic steradians of the solar magnetic field to be around $10^{18}$ ergs for the 2.8 GeV energy threshold, and suggest that the energy released in this vast volume could reach as high as $10^{20}$ ergs for a higher energy threshold of 10 GeV. Furthermore, we found that the ultra-high energy photons flux exhibits an isotropic characteristic in the solar magnetic field, with a predicted interaction energy of $10^{18}$ ergs in the 3.5 billion cubic steradians of the solar corona over a one solar cycle period. Additionally, we observed that the predicted energy of gamma-ray bursts in the 3.2 billion cubic steradians of the Large Magellanic Cloud, based on the solar magnetic field model, amounts to $2.6\pm0.5\times10^{39}$ ergs over a one solar cycle period for an energy threshold of 2.8 GeV. We also examined data from the Alpha Centauri X-ray binary system and the Crab Nebula, but did not detect statistically significant excess flux levels. Our model suggests that the ultra-high energy photons flow in the solar magnetic field could provide the dominant source of energy for the electron flow in the Crab Nebula, with potential implications for nebula luminosity variability. With the proposed model, we predict that the detection of gamma-rays in the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud and other nearby galaxies is imminent, with a statistical significance of more than ten times the typical solar flux levels for a wide range of energy thresholds.

Distributed systems demand robust and efficient data storage solutions that can function across multiple network environments. Replicated data structures have long been the standard for handling large amounts of data in these systems, providing both high performance and reliability. However, implementing such systems is complex due to the risk of conflicts arising from concurrent updates. Many existing solutions tackle this issue, but most are tailored to specific use cases and are highly system-specific. Our research focuses on creating a universal design framework for building replicated data structures that can handle conflicts efficiently. We introduce the Eliminate-Win framework, addressing the fundamental challenges of replicated data management and developing a suite of practical applications based on it. The framework is highly adaptable, allowing developers to customize its components to suit their particular needs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Eliminate-Win through the design of three conflict-free replicated data structures: a map data structure, a set data structure, and a distributed counter. The performance of these designs is comparable to that of conflict-prone data structures, with map and set data structures showing a conflict rate less than $1\%$ and counter data structures exhibiting a average of $0. Do not remove quote. 99\%$ conflict rates in our testing scenario. The framework and its implementations are available online at this link. Furthermore, we explore the possibilities of integrating Eliminate-Win with other distributed systems technologies and discuss potential areas for future research in this field. The rise of decentralized applications and the growing need for robust data management solutions make the study of replicated data structures more pertinent than ever. As such, we believe that the Eliminate-Win framework will be valuable to the development community, with its modular design and flexible architecture making it suitable for a wide range of use cases and scenarios. Additionally, we anticipate that the framework's efficient performance and low conflict rates will be of great interest to those working on the optimization of distributed systems. Investigating radio sources with flat spectra across multiple size categories should provide insight into their underlying causes, given that both magnetic field properties and electron energy distributions likely vary significantly with source size. To accomplish this, a VLA-LBERT-based method was used for source extraction and flux stacking on 34 fields spanning 0.001 to 72 square radians on the sky. The analysis used 1280 radio sources within a specific size range (0.07 to 3.5 arcseconds) and frequency range (10-30 GHz) for each of seven distinct angular bins. Results show that large sources (>1.4 arcseconds) exhibit larger fluxes than smaller sources, with an opposing trend at larger sizes above 3.5 arcseconds. Additionally, a distinct source type emerges at an angular size of around 0.1 square radians (corresponding to a physical scale of ~10 kpc in a distant radio galaxy), exhibiting enhanced flux density compared to other sources. This distinct source type dominates at larger angular sizes (above 0.3 square radians) in terms of flux density. To explain these findings in terms of source orientation, a model assumes that sources with large apparent sizes are likely viewed at large angles, resulting in extended jet components, whereas sources with small apparent sizes are more likely viewed at shallow angles, revealing their core emission. This model aligns with observations, suggesting that sources with sizes above 0.1 square radians (corresponding to a physical scale of ~1 kpc in a distant radio galaxy) are likely oriented at large angles and exhibit enhanced flux density compared to smaller sources within the same orientation range, confirming the predictions of the jet model. Furthermore, the distinct source type dominating at large angular sizes and distinct electron energy distributions in sources with different sizes provide evidence for the jet model, while variations in magnetic field properties may also contribute to these findings. Finally, the unique characteristics of sources with sizes above 0.1 square radians suggest that such large sources may represent a distinct source type, with enhanced flux density density due to extended jet components, likely resulting from large angle orientations. Bipartite graphs where vertices from one set are connected to multiple vertices from another set have numerous applications and have been extensively studied in various forms. Despite the significance of these graphs, few exact algorithms exist for finding a most congruent coloring, a variant of graph coloring where vertices within the same set are colored identically, especially for the case where one set contains exponentially more vertices than the other. In our research, we develop an algorithm using a new finite-depth approach, specifically a depth of 2, for a most congruent coloring on bipartite graphs with vertices from one set connected to any number of vertices from the other set. This algorithm results in a polynomial-time solution for a most congruent coloring on bipartite graphs where one set contains $n$ vertices and the other set contains $n$ variables expressing any possible truth values, thus demonstrating the effectiveness of a finite-depth approach for solving bipartite graph coloring problems. Furthermore, this algorithm enables us to establish a parameterized algorithm with a polynomial kernel and a running time of $O(2^{k} poly(n))$ for finding a most congruent coloring on bipartite graphs with $k$ distinct variables within one set. This achievement is notable because previous studies on graph coloring have primarily utilized infinite-depth approaches. Our research also provides a new foundation for developing parameterized algorithms on bipartite graphs containing variables. In addition, we investigate various other problems and obtain similar results for several other variants of the bipartite graph coloring, including the case where one set contains a fixed number of distinct variables and the other set contains any number of vertices, the case where one set contains any number of distinct variables and the other set contains $n$ variables expressing any possible truth values, and the case of bipartite positive graph coloring. Our research is an important contribution to the study of graph theory and will provide valuable insights for further research in this field. We then analyze different external force applications and find that forces directed at the foot's center of contact or beyond can significantly improve bipedal stability by maximizing the robot's foot area or extending its stability boundary. We also discover that forces applied to the foot's center of mass or beyond can stabilize the robot more efficiently by minimizing its required reaction force. Building on this understanding, we design a propellant-assisted bipedal foot that combines elements of both natural and machine-based movement, with the aim of creating a more stable and efficient form of bipedal locomotion. This novel foot architecture maintains balance by regulating fluid release rates and achieves optimal performance by finely tuning its internal components, offering a promising solution for bipedal robots to efficiently move heavy loads on uneven terrain. This research provides a foundation for developing a more complex, human-like walking system by addressing key challenges in robot locomotion, such as maintaining balance, generating forward propulsion, and adapting to external forces and terrain irregularities. This work also paves the way for bipedal robots to transport a wide range of objects, from delicate electronics to heavy machinery, by optimizing their foot design for various objects and environments. This is the first study to examine the intricate relationship between fluid dynamics, robotics, and biomechanics in bipedal movement, with implications for the design of more efficient and stable walking systems for humans and robots. In order to minimize energy consumption, modern computer systems employ dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, combining various frequency and voltage levels to achieve optimal performance and reduced energy expenditure. Despite its effectiveness, this technique's benefits are limited by its reliance on fixed voltage-frequency pairs, constraining its effectiveness when dealing with continuously shifting workload characteristics. For this reason, researchers and practitioners use various techniques, such as algorithm and data structure modifications, to exploit available frequency choices and promote smoother workload transitions. However, a fundamental challenge in this process arises from the significant disparity, often in the range of several orders of magnitude, between the frequencies that hardware can manage, which are typically in the GHz range, and those that it cannot, which are in the MHz range. As a result, any attempt to execute tasks at frequencies not supported by the hardware results in failed program execution and, consequently, loss of performance gains. To address this issue, this research introduces a suite of seven microbenchmark-based workloads that can efficiently utilize a range of CPU frequencies, spanning from GHz to MHz choices, for the purpose of evaluating the potential performance gains of computer systems. An initial investigation into this research is presented in the form of a paper that was presented at the 12th ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PLDI 2021). A corresponding implementation in C++ is provided as an open-source contribution, along with guidelines for incorporating this research into existing frequency-aware programming languages through refactoring and type-system modifications. This research is currently being further developed as part of the HyperDegrade project, with a focus on exploring the performance benefits that can be achieved when using a broader range of CPU frequencies. To this end, a new set of workload characteristics has been defined, incorporating a more intricate hierarchy of tasks that are linked by their performance-to-energy ratios, as well as new execution scenarios that take into account different types of data that vary in their access patterns. In the context of Linear Algebra, matrix multiplication holds significant importance due to its widespread applications and the fundamental role it plays in other computationally efficient linear algebra algorithms, particularly for solving systems of linear equations, defining orthogonal projections, and transforming vectors. This study compares sequential matrix multiplication implementation with a parallel OpenCL approach, leveraging the computational capabilities of a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). A GPU implementation of matrix multiplication utilizes thousands of independent processors, allowing for an extremely high degree of parallelism, which is not available in sequential processing. As a result, the paper demonstrates a staggering performance gap between sequential and parallel methods, with the latter achieving speeds up to 1400 times faster than the former. Interestingly, the paper also reveals that for small matrices, the sequential approach can, in fact, outperform the parallel method due to the overhead associated with launching multiple parallel threads. Consequently, in order to further improve the efficiency of matrix multiplication, the paper recommends increasing the number of independent processors available for parallel processing. Finally, the study provides a range of parallel implementation examples using different numbers of independent processors, along with corresponding sequential processing times for matrix sizes up to 1024x1024. Notably, the paper uses a GPU with 32 independent processors and employs a simple parallel implementation strategy, which is worthy of further optimization. To effectively tackle more complex tasks, a team of robots can collaborate by making joint decisions. We focus on a scenario where a network of agents, operating in a fully observable environment, need to decide on actions that maximize their total reward, subject to certain constraints. We generate a standard representation of their action space by applying an appropriate transformation and leverage variational methods to constrain the distribution of their actions, ensuring it adheres to their communication limitations. By applying efficient optimization techniques, we can solve a more complex collaboration problem efficiently. We highlight the generality of our approach by applying it to multiple problem representations and demonstrating the performance of our method compared to uncontrolled collaboration. Moreover, we can integrate our approach with models of the environment and utilize it across various scenarios, including those with constrained state observation and variable task difficulties. We validate our method against a robust set of reference trajectories in simulations and real-world tests. Notably, our method enables fast online planning, critical for high-frequency control systems. We compare our method's performance to off-policy methods and found it to be at least an order of magnitude more efficient. We have made our code publicly available.
