Machine learning models like neural networks have seen significant growth in
accuracy across various tasks, yet their interpretability lags behind.
Reversing this trend demands a deeper exploration of heuristics that enable
neural networks to efficiently capture important patterns in data.
In the realm of linear regression, causal neural networks offer a promising
framework, as they integrate causal graphs to efficiently capture relationships
between variables and facilitate the back-projection of effects to their
underlying sources.
This study delves into the heuristics of causal neural networks by leveraging
their application in linear regression with an integrated graphical model.
The model assumes a linear relationship between inputs and outputs, as well as
a fixed graphical structure that represents variables' pairwise connections
and their relative weights.
The study demonstrates that neural networks' ability to accurately estimate
regression coefficients and learn the underlying graph structure is unaffected by
the presence of noisy variables and redundant edges in the graph.
Furthermore, the ability to estimate coefficients is inversely related to the
number of independent variables, whereas the ability to learn the graph
structure is inversely related to the number of edges in the graph.
In contrast, an empirical analysis reveals that neural networks' performance
exhibits a more complex interplay when the graph is learned from data, as their
ability to recover the underlying structure is subject to edges that are too
weak or too strong in influencing the target variable.
In such cases, the learning of the graph is essentially the learning of a
monotone Boolean function, for which neural network models are known to perform
poorly compared to other methods.
In practice, this implies the ineffective learning of edges with small weights
or those located in deep paths.
To address this limitation, the study proposes an alternative neural network
model that learns the underlying causal graph through a binary classification
heuristic, for which the code is publicly available. The model's performance is
evaluated under different independent variables, edge weights, and noise levels
in both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in
graph recovery over the baseline model. The study's findings are also supported
by an analysis of the theoretical limitations of neural network models in recovering
causal graphs. The study's results suggest that modern neural network models
excel at learning causal graphs only when the relationships between variables are
linear, the graph structure is fixed, and variables are fully connected, failing
to generalise to more complex scenarios, real-world datasets, or scenarios in
which variables are only partially connected

In the context of Assured Artificial Intelligence, modeling uncertainties is a critical step to ensure that confidence levels reflect the limitations of knowledge and the uncertainties of data. Open-world scenarios pose additional challenges due to the constant influx of new information, which can significantly impact existing knowledge and uncertainty estimates. A major obstacle in uncertainty management is the distribution shift problem, which occurs when new data is drawn from a different probability distribution than the initial training data. As a result, traditional closed-world uncertainty models, such as Gaussian distributions, often fail to capture the complexities of uncertainty in open-world scenarios. In contrast, we propose an energy-based uncertainty model that leverages deep latent representations to capture the complexities of uncertainty in open-world scenarios. This model utilizes a deep latent space to encode both input data and uncertainty levels, and uses a deep metric learning approach to model the energy function governing these representations. By employing deep latent structures, such as manifolds and layers, our model effectively manages the complexities of uncertainty in open-world scenarios. Furthermore, we investigate two open-world uncertainty tasks: (1) distinguishing reliable and unreliable data, and (2) predicting uncertainty levels for new data. By integrating our energy-based uncertainty model with deep learning techniques, we achieve superior performance compared to traditional closed-world uncertainty models. Moreover, our results demonstrate that deep latent structures, such as manifolds and layers, outperform flat representations in various uncertainty tasks. Additionally, we explore the efficacy of our model in assuring artificial intelligence by evaluating its performance under changing data distributions and real-world scenario simulations. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our research on future assured AI research, while also outlining potential research directions for open-world uncertainty modeling. Ultimately, we hope that our work will contribute to the development of more robust assured AI frameworks capable of managing complex uncertainties in open-world scenarios. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation environments and benchmark tasks. To address the need for more comprehensive evaluation frameworks in reinforcement learning, we are introducing Lifelong Evaluation (LL2Eval), a comprehensive set of challenges designed to assess the performance of continual reinforcement learning methods. LL2Eval combines multiple evaluation environments, carefully curated datasets for metric learning, and standardized evaluation protocols to ensure consistent and reliable comparison of different continual learning approaches. The framework is highly adaptable to accommodate various types of tasks, learning scenarios, and evaluation metrics, making it an invaluable resource for researchers working on lifelong reinforcement learning. To facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing, we are introducing a new forum for researchers to contribute their own evaluation environments and challenges to the field. This integrated framework is the result of an ongoing research project, and all related code and resources are part of an open-source repository. In dynamic ecosystems with multiple timescales, identifying early warning signs for significant population changes is crucial, but it is often complicated by long-term fluctuations masking short-term dynamics. This study focuses on a model consisting of two species with different population cycles and varying persistence properties to examine how its behavior changes over time. By determining the model's equilibrium solutions and phase paths, we can predict population trajectories and determine the conditions under which they switch between stable equilibrium solutions. To account for measurement errors in data collection, we modify the model to incorporate observation errors and estimate its parameters using the likelihood function. By analyzing the model's performance with simulated data, we can determine how the complexity of fluctuations influences our ability to detect early warning signs and recover the model's parameters. However, detecting population shifts in actual data sets, such as those for lemmings and vole populations in Norway, proves more challenging due to the magnitude of short-term fluctuations. Nonetheless, our research provides a theoretical framework for identifying early warning signs in dynamic ecosystems. Furthermore, the model is relevant to the longer ecological phenomenon known as the Northern Atlantic Oscillation, or NAO, and its subcomponent, the Scandinavian NAO, or sNAO. By combining our model with NAO data from Norway, we can better understand the impact of external environmental factors on vole population dynamics. This research is an extension of previous studies on the dynamics of vole populations in Norway, particularly those conducted by Gilg and Merriennne, Hanssen and Eriksson, and Bjornstad and Gilpin. In those studies, researchers analyzed population data in Norway to understand the underlying mechanisms driving population cycles, detected duality in population dynamics, and identified early warning signs for significant population changes. Recent studies have found that the star formation rate (SFR) in massive galaxies falls with mass, contrary to the widely accepted notion of a positive correlation between SFR and mass. To comprehend this phenomenon, researchers have examined galaxy bulges and disks separately. The analysis reveals that the SFR in bulges decreases with mass, while the SFR in disks remains unaffected by mass up to $10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$. This distinction helps explain the observed negative correlation between SFR and mass in massive galaxies. Furthermore, the turning point at $10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$ in the specific star formation rate (sSFR)-mass relation can be explained by the transition from disk-dominated galaxy formation at lower masses to bulge-dominated galaxy formation at higher masses. The data also indicate that bulge formation is more efficient in low-mass galaxies with slower sSFR, contributing to the decline in sSFR with mass. The sSFR in massive disks is suppressed due to the impact of bulge formation, which is consistent with the observed positive correlation between sSFR and mass up to $10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$. The turning point in the sSFR-mass relation can also be explained by the effect of major mergers on sSFR, with sSFR decreasing with mass as mergers become more frequent at higher masses. The observed positive correlation between sSFR and mass up to $10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$ can be attributed to the balance between star formation and mergers, with sSFR increasing with mass below this point due to the greater impact of mergers over star formation. The data further show that the mass range of the sSFR-mass turnover is shifted to higher masses for quiescent galaxies and lower masses for star-forming galaxies, with bulge formation the primary driver of this shift. The effect of major mergers on sSFR also contributes to the observed differences in the mass range of the turnover for star-forming and quiescent galaxies. The data also provide new insights into the role of gas fraction in determining the observed negative correlation between SFR and mass in massive galaxies. To speed up sentiment analysis development for understudied languages, researchers have been exploring cross-lingual sentiment analysis approaches that leverage resources from other languages. A key challenge in this area lies in sentiment inconsistencies across different languages, which can result in poor performance on tasks requiring cross-lingual sentiment analysis. To tackle this issue, previous studies have proposed various methods, such as using multiple low-cost tasks to enhance sentiment learning or implementing techniques to synchronize sentiment taxonomies. However, these methods have not been extensively tested for languages other than English. Our research focuses on evaluating and expanding the scope of cross-lingual sentiment analysis to new languages, using the SentiWordNet as a reference sentiment knowledge base. We evaluated multiple models and training settings to determine their effectiveness at resolving sentiment discrepancies and improving sentiment prediction on unseen data. Our findings showed that both multilingual baselines and our proposed models can learn from data with SentiWordNet, but only certain models and training settings proved successful. We further found that, even with successful models, there is significant room for improvement in cross-lingual sentiment analysis compared to supervised approaches. To mitigate the scarcity of labeled data for fine-tuning, we explored whether multilingual pretraining and unsupervised sentiment annotation can enhance the baseline sentiment scores without compromising the learned ability to follow linguistic cues. Our results indicated that both multilingual pretraining and unsupervised sentiment annotation can contribute to better sentiment scores while preserving linguistic awareness, and that combining these techniques yields the best results. Interestingly, we observed that the benefits of multilingual pretraining are more pronounced on languages closer to English, whereas the benefits of unsupervised sentiment annotation follow a geographic distribution that mirrors the distribution of web content. Our findings provide valuable insights for cross-lingual sentiment analysis research, highlighting both the progress made so far and the significant challenges that remain to be addressed. Our work also paves the way for exploring other multilingual tasks that can benefit from multilingual pretraining and unsupervised annotation, while being mindful of the potential risks of confounding factors, such as linguistic biases, that can mask or mimic performance gains. Our research data, models, and code are freely available for download at https://github.com/andersonbrito-crossling/sentiment-multiple-tasks. Our paper is also available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01683. Updated code can be found at https://github.com/andersonbrito-crossling/sentiment-multiple-tasks-updated. The detection of visual relationships has encountered a significant challenge that hinders its further improvement: the issue of erroneous positives. As the number of false positives increases with the number of classes, it significantly reduces the effectiveness of subsequent tasks that rely on these relationships. The primary source of this problem is the class imbalance present in the training data. To address this issue, researchers have been balancing the data through oversampling the negative examples and undersampling the positive ones, yet these techniques fail to tackle the inherent class imbalance present in the dataset. Furthermore, they do not consider the diversity within each relationship class. Our proposed approach, Balanced Sample Distribution, successfully mitigates the issue of erroneous positives by first segmenting the relationship classes based on their diversity and then balancing the distribution of samples within each category. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods on the Visual Genome dataset, reducing the false positive ratio by 25% and the mean average precision by 1.3%. The code for our model has been made available on the MMCV code archive under the label VRD task. Additionally, we have released an open-source tool that allows users to balance sample distribution within each class on any dataset. This technique can also be applied to other classification tasks that involve balancing the detection of diverse categories. The name of the tool is BDD and it is available on GitHub under the MIT license. The goal of our research is to enhance the detection of visual relationships by minimizing the number of erroneous positives. As a result, we have introduced an evaluation metric called precise mean average precision (PMAP). The PMAP metric offers a more accurate representation of the relationship detection task by prioritizing the reduction of false positives over the increase in true positives. One of the main challenges in designing efficient hardware accelerators lies in effectively utilizing available concurrency within processing tasks. To overcome this, a novel approach is presented here, where the data itself serves as the trigger for concurrent processing. This concept, known as "Data Addressable Concurrent Processing", is characterized by three key features: first, data is given a unique address to function as a trigger; second, multiple processing pathways are enabled simultaneously, each triggered by specific data; third, a separate memory space is allocated for data to facilitate independent access. This framework is exemplified through the development of a real-time image processing application, showcasing significant performance gains when compared to conventional hardware approaches. Specifically, a Data Addressable Concurrent Processing implementation on an FPGA achieved a frame processing rate of 120fps, outperforming a sequential software version by 150x and surpassing a conventional hardware equivalent by 5x in terms of processing power. This data-driven processing methodology holds promise for enhancing the efficiency of hardware accelerators in various computational domains. To validate this approach, an evaluation framework comprising four aspects is employed to assess the Data Addressable Concurrent Processing framework, yielding favorable results for all aspects. Ultimately, this research is expected to inform the design of future Data Addressable Concurrent Processors through the insights gained from this case study. This approach is applicable across different programming languages and is currently being explored for potential integration into Domain Specific Languages to optimize hardware acceleration. The challenges and solutions outlined here are expected to be relevant in the context of near-future hardware platforms. We analyze three-dimensional, force-based simulations of fifty-seven galaxies within the $z=2.9$ galaxy cluster, observing how their bulges and disk shapes develop over time. These simulations, with a resolution of several kiloparsecs, model the galaxies' interactions within the cluster by incorporating gravitational tidal forces and supercomputer-generated streams of accreting gas. We focus on how quiescent galaxies' bulges and disk shapes are affected by major mergers, star formation, accretion, and tidal forces. Our findings show that galaxies with lopsided disks undergo significant bulge growth without shrinking, attributed to the conversion of kinetic energy due to tidal interactions. This is in contrast to major mergers, which cause quiescent galaxies to shrink and form bulges through shock-induced star formation. We also discover that lopsided interactions trigger star formation and bulge expansion, accompanied by changes in a galaxy's central density. Moreover, we find a strong correlation between bulge growth and the rate of star formation, independent of tidal effects. Lopsided interactions are responsible for the majority of bulge development in these galaxies, accounting for over half of all bulge growth. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that tidal interactions can result in the formation of bulges without shrinkage, providing insight into the early universe's galaxy population and challenging traditional one-to-one star formation ratios. Building on our previous work, we update the growth of bulge-to-disk ratios and explore alternative models for quiescent galaxy evolution. Due to the importance of lopsided star formation, we propose revising the well-known specific star formation rates and 1:1 star formation ratios in quiescent galaxies, with implications for the eshaped quenching model and our understanding of the universe's cosmic downsize effect. Furthermore, our findings suggest that galaxy evolution is influenced by their intrinsic asymmetry, with long-lasting lopsided motion playing a crucial role in the development of bulges and disk shapes. Consequently, we predict that similar ratios of bulge growth to star formation and bulge expansion due to central mass aggregation should also be observed in other galaxy populations, such as those in the $z=3$ galaxy clusters, with effects on the shape of the fundamental plane of quiescent galaxies. Lastly, our research on the interplay between accretion, star creation, and morphological alteration in quiescent galaxy clusters provides a framework for investigating the early universe's galaxy population, with implications for the evolution of galaxy clusters like Coma. We examine a nonlinear elliptic equation that represents the formation of singularities for the Davey-Stewartson equation under specific boundary conditions. By applying variational methods, we find solutions in a bounded domain as its perimeter $T$ approaches infinity. Due to the equation's symmetry, we can reduce the problem to a one-dimensional variational approach along circles. The identified solutions exist when the domain's presence is taken into account and exhibit distinct features for odd and even values of $T$. A secondary application of a local minimization technique helps us analyze these solutions' properties and whether they are periodic within the domain. Our findings also reveal how the number of peaks in these solutions changes as $T$ increases. Ultimately, we establish conditions under which these solutions become modulated and periodic within the domain. Our work extends previous research by Guo and Shervarathy to a broader class of functions and includes additional results. A key aspect of our proof involves establishing a variational formulation for these solutions that connects them to a one-dimensional Hamiltonian system. By relating our equation to a Hamiltonian system with a periodic boundary condition, we can leverage existing results to prove the second mountain pass character of the functional and thus the existence of these solutions. Our work has been initially reported in the paper 'Presence, individuality and periodicity of bubbling solutions for a critical nonlinear elliptic equation' presented at the 13th AIMS Conference on Dynamical Systems and Applications, held in Madrid, Spain from July 2019. This study confirms that the linearized equations derived from viscous relativistic hydrodynamics accurately predict waves with speeds of sound $c_s=1$ (in appropriate units) and $3c_s^2$ for first- and second-order perturbations respectively. Additionally, $c_s$ remains consistent across all waves, including shear and heat modes. An explicit formula for the damping rates of these waves was obtained. It is noteworthy that the dispersion relations and damping rates were independent of the specific shock hydrodynamics equations used. A notable finding was that the second-order perturbation theory failed to yield a distinct heat mode component, which then became apparent only upon analysis of the full hydrodynamics equations. A notable aspect of this research was the development of a formal framework for verifying the linearized equations across various relativistic hydrodynamics theories. This framework involves analyzing the hydrodynamics equations in a systematic manner to identify relevant waves and derive their linearized equivalents. This work is a direct follow-up to Foster and Roper, J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 2020. These findings are relevant to previous studies by Foster and Roper, J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 2020, Keil, Phys. Furthermore, this research provides a solution to the previously raised issue by Keil, Phys. Rev. C 2001. Finally, this work demonstrates that the linearized equations derived from the full hydrodynamics equations resemble those proposed by Ritter, Phys. Rev. C 2009 and Ropert, Phys. Rev. C 2010, 2010 for weak shocks, which is expected given that both are first-order theories. In contrast, this research shows that both second-order theories, namely HRHDD and NRHDD, accurately predict waves with speeds of sound $c_s=1$ and $3c_s^2$ for first- and second-order perturbations respectively. In this work, a novel anomaly detection framework in quantum machine learning is introduced, centered on the concept of measurement-based data sampling. This framework is designed to identify and mark data points whose underlying functional characteristics change when collected under different sampling regimes. Specifically, it pinpoints data points that behave differently when sampled with increasing precision. This advanced capability enables the exploration of intricate functional landscapes by gradually refining the precision of data collection. As a key feature, this approach is robust to common noise fluctuations. To demonstrate its effectiveness, in-depth analytical and numerical evaluations are conducted. Furthermore, in-depth case studies are provided to illustrate in practice how this method can be employed to guide the development of efficient hyperparameter tuning strategies for complex optimization problems. The source code for this project is publicly available on GitHub under the MIT license. Additionally, a companion Jupyter notebook is available with interactive visualizations. This research was supported by the National Research Council of Canada and the Canada Council for the Arts. The authors would also like to express their gratitude to the University of Ottawa for providing computational resources. The work presented in this paper has been submitted to the journal Neurocomputing and is awaiting review. Therefore, this initial report will serve as the manuscript.

Historically, this issue was addressed by Goldwasser and Kalai through the concept of "don't trust -- verify" decryption methods. A new construction of coercion-resistant digital signatures builds upon their ideas, offering an adaptable solution to several problems involving encrypted communication in the presence of coercion. However, our analysis reveals that previous results on decryption methods were incomplete, leading to an exploration of additional classes of protocols susceptible to coercion. This achievement builds upon previous work by Hermann and Pancoast, who demonstrated the applicability of a PTAS for certain instances of CSPs on sparse domains; however, their proof lacked a comprehensive explanation. In recent years, deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various pattern recognition tasks, consistently outperforming previous best methods. However, their superior performance is largely attributed to their extensive use of massive datasets and computational power, rather than any inherent superiority over other models. Conversely, when it comes to understanding and explaining their decision-making processes, deep neural networks by nature are opaque and difficult to comprehend. Consequently, significant effort has gone into investigating the internal workings and reasoning behind these networks. One related aspect that has gained considerable attention is understanding how exactly deep neural networks interpret and process visual data. Numerous studies have endeavored to illuminate this aspect by analyzing the network's attention mechanism during image processing. Our study stands out from the crowd by delving into two lesser-studied aspects: how deep neural networks comprehend visual data and what their internal representation entails. Our primary contributions can be summed up as follows: first, we provide empirical evidence that deep neural networks' capacity for understanding visual data varies depending on the task at hand, with some tasks being inherently easy to grasp, while others require a greater degree of visual understanding. Secondly, we attempt to break down the complex internal representation of deep neural networks into its constituent elements by conducting an in-depth analysis of multiple feature extraction techniques. This examination reveals that different deep neural network components focus on extracting distinct low-level and high-level features, with each being a hierarchical representation of visual elements, including primitives, shapes, parts of objects, whole objects, backgrounds, foregrounds, and even abstract concepts. Working with high-dimensional nominal data, we face the challenge of selecting relevant categorical features from a large set of possible attributes. To tackle this issue, we draw on the Group Lasso method but modify the cost function to achieve a more compact and interpretable feature subset. By transforming the data into a series of binary vectors representing category memberships, we apply Group Lasso within a linear regression framework. However, the traditional approach faces limitations due to its rigid adherence to the sparsity axiom, which hinders the inclusion of redundant information in feature subsets. To address this, we propose an alternative formulation that allows for the selection of relevant categories, along with subsets of categories that provide significant information over basic models. Through extensive simulations and real-world experiments, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in feature selection and accurate prediction for high-dimensional nominal data. Notably, our results highlight the subpar performance of conventional Group Lasso in such scenarios, underscoring the necessity of our formulation. Furthermore, our method exhibits particular effectiveness in selecting robust features across multiple runs. The code and data for our experiments are freely available for download. Moreover, we explore and visualize the inherent structure within our proposed formulation by interpreting it as a combination of standard Lasso problems, thereby gaining valuable insights into its behavior. Ultimately, our work offers a compelling case for incorporating diverse information within feature subsets, a concept that warrants further exploration across diverse machine learning contexts. The name "Enhanced Group Lasso" is also proposed as a potential framework for this line of research. The paper is subsequently published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We have developed a biophysical model of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) dopamine neuron function in marmoset monkeys, utilizing a set of distinctive electrical properties associated with these neurons. The model incorporates multiple cellular components including dopaminergic neurons within the SNpc, and accurately reproduces a wide range of marmoset dopamine neuron electrical characteristics, including firing patterns and overall behavior. Given that early-stage Parkinson's disease is marked by the selective loss of these dopaminergic neurons, our model can potentially simulate the abnormal functioning of remaining neurons and provide insights into the underlying causes of the disease's electrical activity patterns. By combining this model with a system containing the marmoset SNpc circuitry and the target striatal nucleus, we can explore how abnormal dopamine neuron firing patterns may contribute to the development of beta oscillations, a hallmark movement abnormality in Parkinson's patients. Our computational model can be validated using recently collected electrophysiological data from marmoset monkeys with Parkinson's-like symptoms, and further optimized to predict the effects of deep brain stimulation on beta oscillations. By incorporating recently developed in vitro recordings of marmoset SNpc dopaminergic neurons, our model is refined to better predict a range of firing patterns that are abnormally frequent in animals with Parkinson's-like symptoms. This research provides a foundation for exploring various Parkinson's disease models and potential treatments through biophysical modeling of the marmoset SNpc dopamine neuron system. Additionally, we outline key challenges and innovative approaches for further modeling the underlying causes of Parkinson's disease. Our research is also relevant to recent initiatives aimed at advancing brain research through computational models and high-performance simulations. We conclude by highlighting the potential for our modeling framework to contribute to several ongoing Parkinson's disease research projects, and by outlining a pathway for further investigation into the role of dopamine neuron properties in Parkinson's disease. Our research is being made available as an open-source project, with a dedicated webpage providing access to all research data, models, and associated discussion forums. This will enable other researchers to contribute to this research, and facilitate the exploration of alternative Parkinson's disease models through computational modeling. Our research is also being complemented by a series of educational lectures on computational modeling of brain function, and on recent advancements in brain research through simulation, as part of an ongoing initiative. This will ensure that the research community remains informed about the progress of this research, and will provide an opportunity for other researchers to contribute to this project. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for optical integral field spectroscopy of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and part of the GOALS sample. These observations were carried out in order to investigate gas dynamics and recover gas balances for these galaxies through ionized gas velocity mapping and SED analysis. Our data was acquired with the KOOLS-IFU's 20.4 x 20.4 arcsec$^2$ field of view and 1.3 arcsec$^2$ spatial sampling, along with 45.44 Å spectral resolution. Our observations of large ionized velocity fields in 3 out of the 9 targets and rotating gas disks in 4 out of them have expanded our understanding of the diverse gas dynamics present in these galaxies. Our study also highlights the capabilities of the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for optical IFU observations, especially in studying a wide range of ultr/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own. Our data will be useful for further research utilizing machine learning algorithms and multi-wavelength analyses to gain even more insights into these fascinating galaxies and their complex dynamics. A new species of neutrinos can affect the universe through its primordial abundance, interacting with other matter only through gravity, and so can a $f(R)$ gravity model, as they all relate to the universe's early history. These two alternative cosmology theories - big neutrino masses and $f(R)$ gravity - are often examined individually within the framework of modified gravity theories; however, it is essential to explore their combined effects on the universe's structure formation. Using a code that accounts for both effects within the parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN) parameters, $\gamma$ and $\beta$, researchers discovered that a combination of large neutrino masses and $f(R)$ gravity could significantly impact the universe's dark matter halo turn-around radii. Compared to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, such a combined scenario results in a mean deviation of 2.5 times that of separate large neutrino masses or $f(R)$ gravity effects. Furthermore, in dense regions, the impact of a combined large neutrino mass and $f(R)$ gravity on the turn-around radius can be as high as 50%. Consequently, if the universe's neutrino mass is found to be substantial, it would indicate that $f(R)$ gravity must also be influential, and thus, alternative gravity theories should be considered to better comprehend the universe's structure formation. Additionally, observing the turn-around radius in high-density regions of the universe can provide valuable insights into the universe's massive neutrino population and $f(R)$ gravity effects. Lastly, in comparison to other structural indicators, turn-around radius can serve as an early marker for structure formation. Therefore, studying the turn-around radius in alternative cosmology and modified gravity theories can offer a more precise understanding of the universe's formation. Ultimately, investigating this phenomenon with upcoming galaxy surveys such as DESI, SCOPE, and SPICA-PSA will allow for a more accurate assessment of the universe's neutrino mass and $f(R)$ gravity behavior. The findings of this research can be verified through observational data on galaxy clusters obtained through cosmic emulators like COLOSIMO, with predicted neutrino masses ranging from 0.06 to 0.11 eV, and an estimate of $f(R)$ gravity parameters based on models such as Dvali-Gabadadze-Polchinski (DGP and LGGP. Therefore, in consideration of its distinct sensitivity to structure formation, turn-around radius can be a promising indicator for evaluating the universe's neutrino mass and $f(R)$ gravity effects

The study also reveals that both temperature and moisture play a crucial role in determining the characteristics of convection, with only the two-cross-sectional-area-fluids model successfully capturing these characteristics. The study further shows that both the traditional model and the two-cross-sectional-area-fluids model exhibit similar skill in forecasting large-scale convection characteristics; however the traditional model exhibits better performance in forecasting minor fluctuations. The study further finds that both models can capture various convection structures, with the results indicating that both models can capture both cellular and plume-like convection structures, with the traditional model exhibiting better performance in forecasting cellular convection structures. We examine whether it's feasible to create genuine entanglement in separate, uncorrelated particles using a single shared source, relying on Jaynes-Cummings interactions. Our investigation involves setting up a quantum network with multiple nodes, each equipped with a two-state atom and a single-mode cavity. We demonstrate that, without imposing correlations on the input states, we can generate genuinely entangled atoms emerging from different cavities, a phenomenon we illustrate through specific examples using pure and mixed states. Notably, we show that certain combinations of unitary Jaynes-Cummings operations can result in the production of highly entangled states, with an emphasis on cat states as a primary example. Furthermore, we establish that a two-mode Jaynes-Cummings interaction is sufficient for creating authentic tripartite entanglement. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for implementing genuine entanglement using Jaynes-Cummings interactions in a scalable and correlation-free manner. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As the next generation of the detector, CMS will undergo upgrades to enhance its performance, particularly in identifying rare processes at the LHC's future operating conditions. The pixel detector, responsible for accurately locating particles with high momentum, is undergoing an upgrade to improve its readout system and front-end electronics. However, the new extended pixel pilot modules introduced in 2017, featuring increased digital precision and a more advanced readout system, pose challenges during the early stages of data processing, known as the edge effect. To overcome these difficulties, a new data processing approach was developed, leveraging side-band regions to estimate and correct for noise in the edge regions. Initial results demonstrate significant improvements in hit recovery at the edge, exceeding the designed hit efficiency threshold, and show that the new processing approach matches the performance of the traditional method in the bulk of the pixel detector. Furthermore, findings indicate that the noise characteristics in the edge region match those in the side-band regions, allowing for efficient noise suppression. The approach is illustrated through a calculation of the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density for the scalar SU(2) glueball within the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) model. The study reveals that the spectral density of the scalar SU(2) glueball is predominantly composed of discrete spikes at values corresponding to the masses of WZW states, in contrast to the continuous spectrum often associated with quantum field theories. The approach is a valuable tool for exploring the internal structure of mesons within non-perturbative quantum field theories. The results suggest that the spectral density of the scalar SU(2) glueball is characterized by spikes at mass values aligned with those of WZW states, providing a deeper understanding of the nature of mesons within the WZW model. organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.

performance of the model. The code for this project has been made publicly

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an independent probe of black hole phase transitions. We further explore this by linking the thermal entropy of the shadow radius to thermodynamic potentials, confirming that non-monotonic behavior can result from non-linear interactions. Ultimately, we conclude that both the shadow radius and thermodynamic potentials can serve as reliable indicators for identifying phase transitions in black holes. Additionally, we demonstrate that the specific heat capacity of the shadow radius exhibits a more intricate structure than its horizon-based counterpart, providing valuable insights for the study of black hole phase transitions. Finally, we illustrate that both thermodynamic potentials and the shadow radius can be utilized to investigate the phase structure of black holes within any gravitational framework. Lastly, we examine how the non-linear electrodynamics parameter influences both the shadow radius and thermal entropy of the shadow, in addition to the specific heat capacity structure. This, in turn, modulates the shadow radius's ability to undergo a phase transition, demonstrating how such transitions can be controlled through adjustments to this parameter. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the value of exploring the thermal properties of black holes in their shadow projections. Furthermore, we contend that both the shadow radius and thermodynamic potentials offer valuable frameworks for delving into the intricate structure of black hole phase transitions, and that such transitions can be both initiated and halted by the non-linear interaction between electromagnetic fields. Consequently, our findings provide a deeper understanding of black hole physics when nonlinear interactions are prevalent, while also highlighting the necessity to broaden the scope of black hole research to encompass their thermal properties as reflected in their shadows. Additionally, such research will contribute significantly to our understanding of black holes in nonlinear contexts, and will also offer valuable insights for exploring the connections between black hole physics and nonlinear phenomena in quantum mechanics, as well as the role that gravitational fields have on such processes. Conversational interfaces have become increasingly popular due to their user-friendliness, and as a result, various conversation systems are being developed to facilitate engaging interactions between humans and computers. Given the complexity of crafting natural responses, it's essential to develop a robust conversation framework that can effectively produce high-quality sentences. Current methods based on generative models are often ineffective, leading to repetitive conversations. In this paper, a open-domain conversation approach is presented that utilizes transformer models to generate human-like responses for any given input. The proposed system is designed with multiple roles to manage different conversation tasks, such as producing initial greetings, developing conversation topics, and creating final goodbyes. To optimize the system, a semi-automatic evaluation method that combines human and automatic assessments is employed to rate the naturalness of generated sentences. The system's performance is tested with two different transformer models, and its efficiency is compared to that of a baseline conversation system. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms the baseline in naturalness, while also showcasing the influence of model size on conversation naturalness. Notably, our approach achieves comparable naturalness to human-conversational systems but with significantly reduced human assessment costs. The proposed system's code and data are publicly available on GitHub. In particular, our implementation of the conversation data dataset is available at https://github.com/ghr96/open-domain-conversation-data and an example of the UI is available at https://github.com/ghr96/open-domain-conversation-ui. Finally, the results of 20 human evaluations are available alongside the proposed system's models on arXiv. In contrast to current human-computer interaction systems that rely on pre-defined questions, the proposed system offers a more flexible and user-friendly experience. In addition, the dataset created for this research has the potential to contribute to advancements in both conversation and game development technologies. In particular, the dataset's diversity could facilitate the development of more realistic game environments, while its large size presents a challenge for current generative models, making it essential to explore novel methods for efficiently training transformer models on large datasets. In terms of future work, incorporating multiple language support and adapting the proposed system to mobile devices are key areas for further research. In conclusion, this research has demonstrated the potential for open-domain conversation systems to provide human-like interactions by leveraging large language models. As such, it is essential to address the challenges faced by these systems, such as maintaining natural language engagement over extended periods. The growing popularity of 360-degree (360-degree) video viewing is providing an engaging travel experience for users, but the current text-based search functionality falls short in helping them plan their viewing. To address this, our research introduces an innovative concept called caption-based viewport forecasting, which enables pre-viewing destination exploration in 360-degree travel videos. By analyzing caption data corresponding to specific viewing areas, our network learns to predict related captions for areas that have not been viewed. Our prototype application demonstrates exceptional performance in forecast accuracy, outperforming non-deep learning competitors. Moreover, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art 360-degree viewport change detection methods. With minimal reliance on audio, our method effectively handles noisy and distracting background sounds. Our research provides valuable data and a modular framework for integrating viewport prediction functionality into existing 360-degree video players. Experimental evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach on various travel videos. Furthermore, user assessments confirm the usability and engaging nature of our 360-degree video viewer. In contrast to linear video viewers, our results reveal differences in user perception. Overall, our study paves the way for the development of more interactive and engaging 360-degree travel video services. A companion website featuring our application is available at https://caption360.cs.washington.edu/. The study's formal reproduction, along with additional details, can be found in a published manuscript available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04044. With the continuous surge in 360-degree video viewing, our research aims to create an innovative, user-friendly, and interactive travel experience for viewers to explore before watching the video. To this end, our approach combines caption data with low-rank matrix factorization to anticipate related captions for unviewed areas, demonstrating superior performance over competing methods. The implementation, comprising a prototype application and experimental evaluations, showcases high forecast accuracy and user satisfaction, setting a new standard for 360-degree video viewing. As such, our work has significant implications for the further integration of audio and visual elements in 360-degree video travel guides to enhance the viewing experience. Although our research focuses specifically on travel videos, the proposed approach can be adapted to predict viewport changes in other 360-degree video applications. The study's results support the idea that machine learning algorithms and low-rank matrix factorization, in particular, are well-suited for this type of prediction task. The fact that our evaluation shows differences in user perception for linear and interactive 360-degree video viewers suggests that more research is needed to fully understand user preferences in this context. Tensor network representations of physical systems have proven useful in understanding their behavior and properties. However, standard tensor network methods can lose precision when describing thermal equilibrium states and temporal evolution, which is because these techniques typically involve approximations that distort the system's algebraic structure. To address this issue, we developed a novel tensor network formulation that maintains local precision when modeling thermal mixed-states and temporal evolution. This new framework draws from the matrix product operator formalism and incorporates the algebraic structure unique to each system through a set of localized tensors. By applying this approach to examples like the XXZ spin chain and massless Dirac fermions, we demonstrated its effectiveness in obtaining reliable results for thermal correlations, response functions, and temporal evolution even near equilibrium and for arbitrary time intervals. Furthermore, this method allows for the integration of time-dependent driving terms and quench scenarios. Notably, we observed how the precision of this tensor network algorithm compares favorably to other methods, especially in the summer regime. Additionally, we explored connections to stochastic diagram expansions, revealing that this algorithm's Monte Carlo simulations equate to interacting tropical lattices, which provides insight into its efficiency. Overall, this new tensor network formulation offers enhanced accuracy and is a more versatile tool for studying temporal evolution and thermal states in quantum systems. It is also expected that this approach will be adaptable to studies of closed systems and used in investigations of non-equilibrium phenomena in two-dimensional systems. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration changes known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's thermal protection layer expanding and contracting. The number of glitches detected varied based on defined threshold standards and their potential influence on the experiment's outcome was assessed. A statistical analysis of available data suggested that glitches have a negligible impact on the most reliable measurements of acceleration. Therefore, the inherent flaws in the satellite's construction may not significantly impede the ability to accurately test the weak equivalence principle. The actual data collected by the Microscope experiment has shown results consistent with its theoretical predictions. The minimum strong shortest route union cover problem has been well-examined in recent years, with various generalizations and restrictions being researched. This study specifically explores the k-Strong Shortest Route Union Cover problem on a set of specific graphs, including complete graphs, where the objective is to determine if there exists a subset of k strongest shortest routes that can cover all paths. Additionally, this study examines the k-SSRUC problem within the context of specific network types, such as series-parallel networks and planar networks, and investigates the conditions under which a cover by the k strongest shortest routes exists. Furthermore, this study delves into the complexity of determining the minimum strong shortest route union cover for a specific graph or network, and either provides a general bound on the number of required routes or a characterization of the optimal solution in cases where it is computationally tractable. Finally, this study also examines the k-SSRUC problem with respect to its parametric complexity. In particular, this study investigates how the complexity of the k-SSRUC problem changes in response to an increase in the value of k, and explores whether a cover by the k strongest shortest routes exists in a graph. The results of this study provide insights into the k-SSRUC problem, and can be applied to fields such as logistics, medicine, and telecommunications. The methods employed in this study involve both graph theoretical techniques, such as edge-or vertex-orientation and reduction, as well as general parametric complexity analysis. The findings of this study have been previously presented at the 11th Annual International Conference on Graphs and Optimization, the 15th Annual Conference on Theory and Applications of Graphs, and the 17th Annual International Conference on Graphs and Optimization. The preliminary results of this study have also been published in the Journal of Discrete Mathematical Sciences and the Journal of Mathematics. Theorems presented in this study can be found in Appendices A to D. The definitions and notations used throughout this study are consistent with standard graph theoretical terminology, and all edge-orientations referred to in this study are assumed to be strong. Due to the extensive nature of this study, a concise overview of the k-SSRUC problem is provided in Section 1, along with a review of the relevant literature in Section 2. The novel contributions of this study are then outlined in Section 3. As the number of frogs grows on an infinitely old critical Galton-Watson tree, its essential density over time has been shown to converge to a specific value. We demonstrate that this limiting density equals the probability that a path in the tree, starting from the root, eventually reaches every branch by a distance of one from its leaf nodes. This result applies to a general class of branching processes where the number of offspring per node varies randomly. We introduce the concept of near-optimal mimicry and develop a new model for mimicry learning that differs from existing paradigms. In our model, we leverage labeled data from a diverse set of tasks to train a teacher model. The goal for the student model is to perform optimally on a specific task using data from a separate set of task-specific labeled samples that are significantly smaller than the initial diverse data. We investigate two variants of our near-optimal mimicry learning problem, depending on whether the student has access to additional unlabeled task-specific data. For the second variant, we show near-optimal mimicry learning is feasible with unlabeled data but the solution requires more complex algorithms than our TRAIL solver. In collaborative settings between robots and people, learning from unmarked demonstrations could enhance their performance by allowing them to learn from casual, non-expert feedback. This research enables a robot to learn from unmarked demonstrations to calibrate its camera and estimate the position of its end-effector in a 3D space using a stereo camera and a wrist-mounted camera. A movement prediction model is trained to predict the 3D trajectory of objects being grasped and a 6D pose estimation model is used to determine the position of the end-effector by matching predicted 3D trajectories with observed ones, resulting in multiple possible solutions which are then refined through interaction with the environment and finally selected based on their consistency with actual sensor readings. Experiments show that our method effectively learns from a small number of unmarked demonstrations on various objects and in different scenes. Notably, it learns to adjust its camera and estimator without the need for calibration or specific labels. Additionally, through the use of a manipulation dataset, it is demonstrated that our method generalizes well to novel objects and selects the most physically plausible end-effector positions. A key aspect of this work is the incorporation of a technique to assess the reliability of sensor data, generating a new dataset that represents unreliable readings and highlights the importance of considering such outliers in 6-DoF pose estimation. This research has implications for the development of more flexible and adaptable robot learning algorithms that can efficiently utilize a wide range of feedback from human collaborators. Quantum financial systems, stemming from the intersection of quantum mechanics and finance, offer novel insights by incorporating elements of uncertainty into financial instrument pricing. In this paper, we introduce the QFS-area concept, a dynamic quantity representing the intersection of a quantum stock price path and the price range specified by a given probability, along with its corresponding characteristics. By defining the probability density function of the QFS-area, we can extract key properties, including mean values that can be used to calculate expected returns and volatility values, providing a framework for assessing risk. Furthermore, by formulating the probability distribution function of the QFS-area, we can leverage extreme value theory to analyze rare event occurrences, such as stock price extreme values. These rare event occurrences can lead to significant financial gains or losses, making it essential to model their behavior accurately. By modeling the QFS-area, we can develop strategies for portfolio optimization, considering both the probability of gaining or losing money and the associated risks. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the quantum stock price, its corresponding variance, and the probability of a price range being crossed over time. By analyzing this relationship, we can gain insights into stock price behavior and make informed decisions about investment duration and potential returns. Overall, the QFS-area provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating and managing risk in quantum financial markets, providing opportunities for significant financial gains through optimized portfolio investment. Furthermore, this framework can be applied across various financial markets, such as foreign exchange and commodity markets, enabling the development of more effective risk management strategies. In the context of portfolio management, multiple stock prices can be modeled using the principles outlined, enabling the optimization of portfolio performance and risk levels. Additionally, this framework facilitates the creation of financial instruments with defined payouts based on specific stock price trajectories, such as trajectory-dependent options, which can provide returns on investment up to 100 times that of traditional options. The potential returns on investment derived from optimized portfolio investment and the development of advanced financial instruments far outweigh the costs associated with quantum simulation, making quantum finance a highly profitable and viable field. The principles outlined in this paper can be applied across various fields, such as the optimization of complex systems, the solution of nonlinear differential equations, and the analysis of time-series data. Furthermore, the extreme value theory and probability distribution properties outlined in this paper can be used to investigate rare event occurrences in these areas, potentially uncovering new insights and revealing novel applications for quantum finance. The research outlined in this paper can be further expanded upon, with potential avenues for investigation including the modeling of multiple stock price trajectories

We investigate the word problem for the R. Thompson group V, exploring its complexity in relation to the length of the given words. Our analysis reveals that any potential shortening of words would imply a significant, nearly quadratic improvement in the complexity of the word problem, specifically achieving a polynomial of degree less than two. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of words with a complexity that is at least proportional to the square root of its order. Furthermore, we show that for almost all elements in V, the complexity of their presentation is at least the square of their order, with the notable exception of the generators themselves, which provide a complexity that is directly proportional to their order. This research provides a new perspective on previous studies concerning the complexity of the word problem in R. Thompson groups. Furthermore, we explore the complexity of the length of geodesics within V, establishing that its complexity is at least the square root of the length of the geodesic. This analysis contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate properties of the word problem in R. Thompson groups. We present preliminary research findings from the LAMOST Time-Domain Exploration survey. Specifically, we analyzed four $K$2 plates from the LAMOST DR7 database, focusing on variable stars. Our team members, including Xianfei Zhang, Zhiwei Chen, and Xiangyan Wang, contributed to this study. Our work identified 506 unique variables across the four $K$2 plates. From the analyzed data, we constructed light curves using the LAMOST spectra and mapped their characteristics. Our research revealed that the majority of variables exhibited periodic luminosity changes, with periods spanning a few days to several decades. We also observed significant diversity in their amplitudes and spectral types. Our analysis suggested a correlation between orbital period and luminosity period, with possible links to mass transfer and binary star types. Our study paves the way for a larger investigation into the LAMOST time-series spectroscopic database. MongoDB, a popular NoSQL database, utilizes document-level transactions to maintain data consistency. Given the complexity of these transactions, ensuring integrity is crucial but also poses challenges. As a result, detecting transactional integrity issues has become an important task in database debugging. This paper introduces an innovative approach, combining static analysis and dynamic validation, to identify inconsistencies caused by concurrent transactions in MongoDB. Our method leverages the MongoDB Java Driver to create a virtual database environment and employs static analysis to minimize the set of transactions that need to be re-run during the debugging process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the MongoDB "isMaster" collection and reporting the performance of our method. Furthermore, we provide our approach as a transactional debugger called "ShardIt", which can be used with the MongoDB Java Driver. The source code of ShardIt is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. Our experimental results show that our method can efficiently detect transactional integrity issues in MongoDB. Additionally, we contribute a dataset of benchmarked applications, demonstrating the practical challenges of transactional integrity issues in MongoDB. This research fills a gap in the field by introducing a transactional integrity validation approach for MongoDB and providing a method for concurrent data management verification. We present the findings of a nuclear forward scattering study on Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ at elevated pressures, which reveals that this material exhibits ferromagnetic behavior under pressure, in contrast to its room-temperature orthoferrite structure where it displays antiferromagnetic properties. Our study finds that a sudden transition from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic ordering occurs when the temperature is decreased below 103 K under high-pressure conditions. Additionally, we observe that the magnetic moment shows a significant increase with pressure, reaching a maximum value of 1.04 $\mu_B$ at 2.5 GPa. This enhancement of magnetic moment with pressure is attributed to the contraction of the material's lattice, which reduces the magnetic exchange interaction and increases the magnetic moment. We also analyze the effects of pressure on the material's lattice parameters, identifying a correlation between the TiO$_8$ anti-tetrahedral distortion and the material's magnetic ordering. Notably, Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ exhibits unique pressure-dependent behavior in comparison to other members of the Aurivillius Bi$_{2n+1}$FeTi$_n$O$_{3n+3}$ series, suggesting that its four-layered structure contributes to its distinct magnetic response to external pressure. Our findings suggest that elevated pressures may be an effective means of inducing ferromagnetic ordering in this material, which has implications for the development of novel ferromagnetic materials through structural adjustments. Ultimately, our study highlights the utility of nuclear forward scattering in investigating the magnetic and structural properties of materials under high-pressure conditions. This technique offers real-time, in-situ analysis of a material's magnetic moment, exchange interaction, and crystal structure - a comprehensive understanding of which is essential for designing novel functional materials. We propose that nuclear forward scattering represents a valuable means of exploring the effects of pressure on materials, which may also be applicable to other in-situ scanning probe microscopy techniques. Furthermore, our results suggest that the Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ system may provide a valuable framework for investigating the interplay between structure, exchange interaction, and magnetic moment in materials subject to external pressure. Additionally, we highlight the need for additional theoretical studies to further elucidate the unique pressure-dependent behavior exhibited by this material. Ultimately, our study underscores the utility of nuclear forward scattering in investigating the magnetic and structural properties of materials under high-pressure conditions, which may also be applicable to other in-situ scanning

Previous research has addressed shortest route problems with both continuous and discrete path components; however, existing duality-based algorithms for solving these problems rely on potentially inaccurate approximations. We develop a more precise dual problem and establish a rigorous error limit for its relation to the original continuous-discrete shortest path problem. The resulting algorithm demonstrates improved accuracy, particularly beneficial in optimizing free flight paths subject to wind constraints. By leveraging the derived error limit, we determine optimal safety margins for navigating to a target using the shortest path despite wind influences. A numerical example illustrating the developed approach in optimal free flight navigation is provided. Furthermore, the article offers a solution for discrete shortest path problems with respect to wind direction. The code for the proposed algorithm has been made available online. We explore the impact of varying wind intensity and a target-reaching criterion on solution strings, establishing a connection to existing methods, including those for continuous wind direction optimization. The article concludes by outlining potential extensions to its results. The developed algorithm is also applicable to discrete shortest path problems with continuous wind direction influences. We investigated the acoustic characteristics of loud noises produced by adhesive tape as it is slowly unwound, focusing on the underlying mechanisms governing these sounds. Our research reveals that the intense sounds emanating from the tape are a consequence of force fluctuations resulting from stick-slip interactions between its layers. We characterized the loud noise as a manifestation of a non-equilibrium, first-order phase transition by analyzing the distribution of sound amplitude and their power spectral densities. Our findings show that the distribution of sound amplitudes conforms to an exponential form, while their power spectral densities exhibit a singular component at a specific frequency, indicative of a non-equilibrium phase transition. Furthermore, we observe that the time it takes for the sound amplitude to reach a certain value increases in proportion to the distance unwound, providing insight into the intrinsic time scales of this process. We demonstrate that the singular frequency contained within the power spectral densities is directly related to the time it takes for force fluctuations to reach a certain equilibrium, and may be influenced by external temperature variations. We explore the effects of varying temperature, uncovering how it influences the distribution of sound amplitudes and their power spectral densities. Additionally, we examine the acoustic characteristics of unwinding tape at different speeds, revealing that increasing the unwinding speed leads to a transition from an exponential to a Gaussian distribution of sound amplitudes. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms producing loud noises when adhesive tape is unwound, and may be applicable to other systems exhibiting similar behavior. We offer a framework for further investigation into noisy systems, and suggest that time-series analysis in conjunction with statistical mechanics can yield a deeper understanding of complex phenomena. We conclude by exploring potential connections between these noise patterns and other phenomena, such as the rhythmic patterns observed in human respiration, providing a foundation for future research into the underlying mechanisms governing these processes. We present a comprehensive analysis of our findings, accompanied by a detailed discussion of our methodology, as well as a thorough examination of the implications of our results. Additionally, we present a concise summary of our findings in the concluding section of this report. The development of cutting-edge laser technology necessitates in-depth understanding of full laser systems, encompassing diode pumps, solid-state lasers, and beam delivery components. This knowledge enables the optimization of system performance, efficiency, and overall operation. However, the intricate nature and diverse origins of these systems pose significant challenges to their reverse engineering, hindrance to the advancement of laser technology through the recovery of obsolete technology. A case study is presented on the enhancement and reverse engineering of a 100 W average power, CPRT (continuously operating, high-power, red-light system) laser used in two-photon microscopy. The original CPRT system featured a complex design with multiple unknown components, which hindered its modification into a green-light system through simple diode-pumped solid-state laser principles. As a result, the need arose to re-engineer the entire system to accommodate a range of output wavelengths. This case study illustrates the intricacies involved in recovering the design of an complex solid-state laser system, highlighting the difficulties encountered and the lessons learned through this experience. The enhanced description of the modified CPRT system, now capable of delivering 2 W of red or green light, serves as an accessible educational resource for the broader scientific community on the intricacies of high-power laser engineering. The recovered design also provides valuable insights for the development of advanced laser technology through the recovery of legacy technology. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the practical utility of reverse engineering high-power laser technology for biological applications, such as two-photon microscopy, by highlighting the significance of system flexibility in output wavelength. The challenge posed by the complexity of these systems also serves as an impetus for the development of open-access educational resources on the inner workings of high-power laser technology. As such, this study contributes to the establishment of an educational platform on the recovery of legacy technology for two-photon microscopy. This platform aims to provide straightforward explanations on the intricacies of high-power laser engineering and to facilitate the recovery of outdated technology to address the technological advancements in microscopy. Given a fixed $p$ with $0 < p \leq 2$, we define an $\ell_p$ space and investigate the behavior of bi-Lipschitz mappings $f$ from subsets of $\ell_p$ to $\ell_p$. Specifically, we explore the properties of bi-Lipschitz mappings $f$ on incompressible subsets $A$ within $\ell_p$, with the goal of determining the minimal increase required for these mappings to be isometric. Our findings reveal that any bi-Lipschitz mapping $f$ from an incompressible subset $A$ within $\ell_p$ must exhibit a significant increase of at least $2^{d-1}$ in its Lipschitz constant, with $d$ representing the dimension of $A$ in cases where $1\le p<2$. However, we demonstrate that this increase is not necessarily achieved by isometric mappings. Moreover, our research establishes that in the scenario where $0 < p < 1$, dimension decrease is evident, with the dimension of $A$ reducing to $d-\lfloor p\log_2(d-1)\rfloor$ for any given $d\ge (1/p)-1$. Conversely, we prove that this dimension decrease is minimal, with $d$ being the smallest possible increase for a bi-Lipschitz mapping from $\ell_p$. Finally, our work also facilitates the extension of these results to Schauder spaces and provides an alternative, more concise proof of previously established results pertaining to the dimension decrease of bi-Lipschitz mappings from incompressible subsets within $\ell_p$ spaces. With these findings, we are able to address and resolve questions posed by Kalton in the field of Banach space theory. Our research is a continuation of prior work conducted by the authors with G. Godefroy and D. Kalton.

To address these shortcomings, we present a novel, lightweight multi-domain cross-sew network architecture, known as MD-CSDNetwork, designed for deepfake detection. By integrating a novel multi-domain cross-sew block that leverages a unique, domain-type-based learning strategy, our model efficiently learns distinct feature patterns across various domain categories without domain-specific training. Empirical evaluations across five domain types, using the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark, reveal that our proposed MD-CSDNetwork outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and processing speed. Furthermore, we showcase the model's capacity to adapt to new domain types with minimal retraining, achieving a notable reduction in errors. Code and model repositories are available at https://github.com/ghr1202/MD-CSDNetwork. With its balance of high accuracy and efficiency, MD-CSDNetwork is poised to become a leading deepfake detection model. Moreover, we contribute a new baseline model, known as CSNetwork, tailored to the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark, achieving a notable detection precision of 73.59%. CSNetwork is also made available in the provided code repository. Nonetheless, it is essential to note that face verification remains a crucial aspect in deepfake detection, with our model exhibiting a notably inferior verification precision of 52.35%, significantly below the standard face verification precision threshold of 80%. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Despite the traditional nature of these scams, research into their digital counterparts is in its infancy. This report on the Forsage cryptocurrency scheme, considered a significant example by industry experts, offers a comprehensive examination of its underlying structure and user behavior. Leveraging data from over 4 million transactions and a survey of over 800 participants, our analysis reveals essential aspects of the scheme's operation, participant levels, and earnings. Our findings demonstrate the irreversible degradation of participant returns, the concentration of wealth among a small elite, and the widespread financial losses among Forsage users. Furthermore, our non-parametric estimation of the scheme's total transaction value is also presented in this report. Forsage is currently under legal investigation and court proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. As such, we refrain from drawing conclusive inferences or making public statements about the scheme's validity. Instead, this report provides an empirical foundation for ongoing research into the economics and sociology of pyramid schemes through smart contracts. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of monitoring and analyzing real-world transactions in the Ethereum network to prevent the resurgence of closed pyramid schemes and to shed light on the behavior of their participants. The data and methods employed in this analysis are also discussed in this report. As the first comprehensive examination of its kind, this study serves as a starting point for exploring other closed schemes as well as potential new ones. As such, we believe that the Forsage case has broader implications for the study of pyramid schemes, the underlying economics of cryptocurrency transactions, and the sociology of participant behavior in decentralized systems.
