This paper proposes a novel concept, shared semantic space, where multiple languages can be represented using a unified dimensional structure. We extract words with similar meanings across languages by grouping them based on their inherent clustering properties. A model is introduced that uses both intra- and inter-lingual information to ensure consistent clustering results. We utilize the K-Means algorithm to achieve this consistency and assign identical cluster labels to equivalent words across languages. Our proposed model includes a method for evaluating the consistency of clustering, achieving this by minimizing the variance of cluster labels, thus ensuring that words with the same label but in different languages are semantically similar. We apply this model to two experiments: one with English and French, and another with English and Chinese. The results show that our model produces cluster-consistent word representations for multiple languages. Notably, by incorporating the clustering algorithm, our model surpasses the performance of existing word representation models in many cases. For instance, our model achieved 65.15% clustering accuracy for English-French, outperforming the next best model by 6.25%. Additionally, our model achieved 62.53% clustering accuracy for English-Chinese, with the next best model at 57.31%. We also observed that the number of clusters has a significant impact on the results, with 100 being the optimal number for both English-French and English-Chinese. Furthermore, by applying a clustering consistency constraint, our model achieved significant improvements in semantic tasks such as word similarity and classification. Our model also demonstrated the ability to generalize to unseen words by leveraging the distribution of cluster centers. Overall, our model successfully constructed a shared semantic space for multiple languages by leveraging both intra- and inter-lingual information, and the code is available at https://github.com/zhengyizhang2017/cluster-consistent-word-representation. This work provides a theoretical foundation for a novel multi-lingual word representation model that can capture both the unique characteristics and shared structures of different languages. Additionally, our model can be applied to various natural language processing tasks that involve generalizing to unseen words. This research is also an exploration into the unique properties of different languages and the underlying reasons for the consistency of clustering results. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable errors in its annotated goal labels. These flaws cause significant performance deviations in current dialogue state tracking models and hinder their potential to ensure operational automation systems' reliability. This paper first analyzes the source of label imperfections in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and then proposes a dataset to assess the robustness of dialogue state tracking models in tolerating annotation mistakes. Additionally, we introduce a newly refined dataset, MultiWOZ 2.0 Revise, aimed at rectifying the original's label issues. Nevertheless, this revised dataset also raises concerns regarding its suitability for evaluating model robustness. Consequently, we introduce an additional dataset, MultiWOZ 2.0 Augment, derived from the original by introducing artificial imperfections. We establish a evaluation metric named Augmented Goal Accuracy to assess a model's performance on this dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate that existing dialogue state tracking models exhibit subpar performance on both the revised and augmented datasets in comparison to the original MultiWOZ 2.0 standard. We believe our research to be a significant contribution in the dialogue state tracking field, specifically in exploring the topic of robustness in the presence of annotation mistakes. In late October 2019, violent demonstrations and widespread unrest broke out in Chile, forcing the government to declare a state of emergency and prompting a mass exodus of tourists from Europe.  We examine this complex societal phenomenon by applying an epidemiological non-local model to represent the spread of information and unrest.  Our analysis focuses particularly on modeling the drastic decline in tourist numbers and incorporates these external influences as periodic fluctuations in a WKBP framework.  Simulated results using the proposed model are compared with actual data for tourist numbers and aggregate unrest levels, showing that the model can replicate the observed patterns and dynamics.  Furthermore, by adjusting model parameters, we explore and predict future behavior under different conditions, providing a theoretical framework for understanding the epidemiological aspects of this societal event.  Additionally, we outline potential extensions to the model to capture additional aspects of the protests, such as government responses and phase shifts in protest scales. Mobile agents require a map of their environment to navigate, and their navigation tools can be either internal (using their sensors to build a map of what they've seen) or external (using pre-built maps along with additional hardware such as GPS). This research focuses on teaching a deep learning model to create a map of its surroundings using sensor data and then use that map to predict the agent's position as it moves. Unlike previous approaches that used a fixed network architecture for both map creation and navigation, this research separates these tasks into two different sub-tasks. This is achieved through the use of an external memory module in the navigation network, allowing it to selectively focus on relevant information in its internal representation when matching it against the map. This is modeled after the attention mechanism used in natural language processing. This approach was tested with a visual-inertial navigation system, a type of mobile sensor platform notorious for its challenging navigation due to the Nav-State estimation requirements. This research implemented a range of defence mechanisms to prevent overfitting, resulting in a high level of accuracy even on unseen data. This method produced results that were significantly better than those of previous approaches, with an average accuracy of 0.161 metres compared to 0.664 metres for the best existing method. This suggests that breaking down mapping and navigation tasks into separate sub-tasks can produce a more accurate outcome. This approach also produced local optimisation, reducing the risk of overfitting. This research used a dataset of 50 minutes of visual-inertial navigation data, collected at a speed of 1.5 metres per second, with 11 different starting points and 11 different ending points, as well as data collected at a faster speed of 3.5 metres per second for 20 minutes. This is the first time a mobile agent has been taught to create a map of its surroundings using sensor data and then use that map to predict its position as it moves. This method produces a higher level of accuracy than existing methods, with an average error of 0.161 metres compared to 0.664 metres for the best existing method. This approach can be applied to a range of mobile sensors, with the visual-inertial navigation system being the most challenging due to its difficult state estimation requirements. This research can be applied to a range of fields including robotics, with the potential to be combined with other sensors such as GPS, as well as being scalable to larger maps, with data collected at a faster speed of 3.5 metres per second for 20 minutes.

This paper introduces the parafermion vertex operator algebra $K(osp(1|2n),k)$, deriving its generators and constructing a basis for irreducible modules within a certain weight range. We establish relationships between $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ and the vertex operator algebra $L(osp(1|2n),k)$, including isomorphisms and duality. The properties of $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ also facilitate the exploration of $L(osp(1|2n),k)$, particularly in cases where $k$ is negative. The entorhinal cortex serves as a key hub within the brain's temporal lobe, with grid cells in its medial portion exhibiting unique properties that facilitate efficient spatial path planning. Research has shown that certain neurons in this region fire in a grid pattern of localized peaks when an animal navigates, and these cells maintain their grid pattern orientation and spacing even as the animal moves. Additionally, some of these neurons, often referred to as "fridge cells," exhibit multiple overlapping grid patterns. Previous studies have examined individual grid cells within this region but have yet to delve into the underlying mechanisms that shape the grid patterns observed across the entorhinal cortex as a whole. This research involves biologically-inspired computational models to emulate grid cell behavior in different parts of the entorhinal cortex. By analyzing these models, our findings suggest to existing theories that the variety of distinct grid patterns seen across the entorhinal cortex can be accounted for by random initial conditions, with subsequent refinement occurring through learning processes that emphasize behavior-based criteria. These computational models exhibit similar performance to their biological counterparts, with characteristics such as grid periodicity, orthogonality, and stability maintained across the cortex. Furthermore, our work introduces novel algorithms capable of generating complex grid patterns, with implications for understanding the brain's neural circuitry. By applying these algorithms to realistic simulations, our results demonstrate that the underlying neural network can produce a diverse range of grid cell firing patterns, with the potential for these patterns to be distinguished by the brain's neural coding principles. This research is conducted using a range of computational tools, with a focus on utilising small neural networks to emulate complex grid cell behavior, and the accompanying theoretical framework is supported by existing empirical data. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the brain's neural code and the development of efficient computational models for navigating complex environments. Additionally, this research showcases the effectiveness of evolutionary and learning algorithms in refining network performance for optimal behavior-based output. The developed models also provide a framework for exploring the brain's neural circuitry and its underlying mechanisms through computational simulations. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the value of integrating biological observations with computational simulations, as well as the benefits of applying real-world constraints to artificial neural networks. As such, this work is relevant to ongoing research in the fields of artificial neural networks, computational neuroscience, and machine learning. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation gradually slows down. Despite this decrease, many mature solar-type stars still exhibit stochastic magnetic activity and likely develop magnetic cycles similar to those seen in younger versions of these stars.  To study these cycles in solar-type stars, we ran numerous simulations of their dynamos, accounting for various rotation patterns, including normal, reduced, and reversed differential rotation.  Our simulations revealed that reduced differential rotation leads to magnetic cycles with shorter periods, consistent with existing empirical estimates.  Conversely, normal and reversed differential rotation patterns result in too long-lasting toroidal magnetic field accumulation, preventing the proper degradation of these fields, thus preventing cycle generation.  This contrasts with solar-like cycle observations, indicating that reduced differential rotation is the most plausible scenario for the cycle generation of slowly rotating solar-type stars.  Furthermore, this study suggests that reversed differential rotation may impede magnetic cycle creation in low-torque magnetically active stars.  The potential for these stars to exhibit magnetic cycles may be assessed with the newly derived criterion:  $\Omega_{polar}/\Omega_{core} > 0.7$.  This research provides a deeper understanding of magnetic cycle generation in slowly rotating solar-type stars.  The obtained results can also contribute to the analysis of potential magnetic cycles in magnetic rotostellar binaries and subgiants.  Future high-resolution spectroscopic stellar activity patterns, along with light curves, can serve as a combined data set for accurately modeling these stars and validating the presented dynamo simulations. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies with different quadratic twists. Our research indicates that the average rank of elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions is less than four. Moreover, under the assumption of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, we find the rank of elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions is determined by a 2-Selmer rank of an elliptic curve in the rational numbers. If the Hasse-Minkowski theorem holds for all global function fields, we demonstrate that the rank of elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions is equal to the number of quartic factors in such extensions. Additionally, under the assumption of BQSD conjecture, we prove that the rank of elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions is equal to the number of quartic factors in such extensions. We provide explicit examples to support our findings. Furthermore, in the case of $S_4$ quartic extensions, we establish that there are infinite sets of elliptic curves with specific rank values, including the smallest known rank five elliptic curves in this context. This paper addresses the challenge of decoding such attacked matrices by assuming the attack affected an entire row of the original matrix. This assumption allows for the reduction of the problem into two more manageable issues under the rank metric. Specifically, given that the attacked row is known only as being linearly independent from other rows, the problem splits into determining the specific independent row and correcting the resulting rank defect. This paper introduces two distinct decoding approaches for this assumed attack scenario, building on existing rank metric decoders. Experimental evaluations, conducted on random parity-check matrices and binary low-density parity-check codes, demonstrate the effectiveness of these decoders in correcting errors under various error rates. Notably, one of the decoders shows improved performance over its conventional counterparts. This improvement highlights the potential benefits of incorporating knowledge about independent rows when designing rank metric decoders. This knowledge could be particularly useful in systems where the distinction between independent and linear rows is known or can be inferred, thereby further enhancing the performance of these decoders. This tradeoff is shown to be influenced by the density of the matrix, with a sweet spot that optimizes this balance for certain matrix densities. The rapid spread of COVID-19 led mobile phone location data to reveal significant changes in human mobility patterns, with varying impacts on different socioeconomic groups. Although there was an initial decline in urban interaction crosswise over cities, a more intricate story unfolded as the pandemic persisted. Referencing mobility data from 137 US cities and nearly 12 million individuals, along with tax return income records, we show that income disparities in urban interactions widened significantly during the pandemic, with initial declines in interactions with those outside one's own socioeconomic bracket followed by even steeper declines in later pandemic stages. Notably, these behavioral shifts in later pandemic stages were disproportionately more pronounced among lower-income individuals, with far-reaching implications for existing urban income inequalities. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that lower-income individuals exhibited smaller mobility radii and fewer cross-socioeconomic interactions further from their residences, with a greater propensity to conform to local public health guidelines. However, these individuals were more likely to deviate from these guidelines when faced with competing demands from family and community, with potential long-term consequences for urban interactions and inequalities post-pandemic. Our research is also complemented by survey data from over 7000 individuals, providing valuable contextual insights into the behavioral shifts observed during the pandemic. Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of examining the complex, stage-dependent effects of public health crises on urban interaction dynamics and inequality. With increasing evidence pointing to the pandemic's exacerbating effect on existing urban income disparities, our research also highlights the critical need for policymakers to develop targeted strategies to mitigate these trends and promote more equitable recovery in post-pandemic urban settings. Mobile robots operating in unstructured environments with varying weather and lighting conditions encounter numerous challenges when navigating using their sonar sensors. These sensors are prone to inaccurate readings due to the presence of debris, foliage, and other obstacles that can cause them to provide misleading information. Furthermore, the slow scanning speed of these sensors means that they often cannot keep pace with the robot's movement, resulting in missed readings and coverage gaps. This paper introduces a new approach, known as immediate sonar blending, which combines the robot's sonar readings with its movement state to produce a consistent and reliable navigation framework. Experimental results with a ground robot demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving the accuracy of its navigation. Furthermore, this paper includes a detailed analysis of the variables that affect the sonar blending algorithm, along with a discussion of the implications of this technique for other navigation systems. This research provides a foundation for optimizing the design of navigation systems that utilize sonar sensors, with potential applications for robots that navigate in environments with obstacles, in fields such as agriculture, construction, and search and rescue. As sonar sensors continue to evolve, with increased scanning speeds and improved accuracy, this approach can be adapted to maximize the performance of these advanced sensors, leading to even more efficient and safe navigation. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, having an effective representation of their surroundings is crucial. In this paper, we introduce HiTMap, a two-layered topological map that utilizes a hierarchical structure to facilitate navigation in unknown areas. The upper layer represents the environment's high-level layout, while the lower layer contains local path planning grids corresponding to specific areas. We demonstrate HiTMap's capability in adapting to changing situations by applying it to a simulation scenario of a mobile robot interacting with moving obstacles and navigating around rotating walls. Our method uses sensory input to update the topological map, and through localization on the HiTMap, we showcase the system's ability to generate efficient, obstacle-avoiding paths for the robot. The code for HiTMap has been made publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, we highlight potential advancements and variations for HiTMap in our concluding discussion. The proposed approach has been analytically assessed for its time complexity, and simulations have been carried out to evaluate the method's performance. The results indicate that HiTMap outperforms a conventional local navigation system in terms of path planning speed. The HiTMap model has been parameterized, and a response surface methodology has been used to optimize its performance. An in-depth analysis of the infrared dark cloud complex, the Dragon, using radio and infrared observations reveals a core with star formation activity within it. Located near the center of this complex, this core, along with several others, was identified through a comparison of radio and infrared data, which showed areas where dust absorption blocks signal transmission. While previous research suggested the Dragon is a molecular cloud complex undergoing dissolution, our analysis suggests the presence of dense cores like the one with star formation activity, providing evidence that the Dragon may not be dissolving after all. By examining how gas and molecules move, as well as the temperature and density of the core, our findings suggest the core is developing into a more stable state, potentially a type of dense, spherical region that can eventually form massive stars. This process is likely being regulated by dynamics rather than gravity, and more observations are needed to better understand the movement of gas within the core. If the Dragon does not break apart, its star-forming regions like the core may continue to shape the surrounding environment. Consequently, the Dragon could become a massive star-forming region, while also offering a unique opportunity to study the development of a massive star-forming region through observations. Furthermore, if the Dragon is a type of molecular cloud complex that can host massive star formation, its structure and process may be similar to those of the G33.61+0.03 complex, which is also forming massive stars. Additionally, the Dragon may be a type of complex that forms when a ring-shaped molecular cloud is pinched by the gravitational pull of an outer ring-shaped magnetic field. If so, the Dragon may provide a unique view into a massive star-forming region that is being shaped by its surrounding environment.

In this study, we examine epistemic modal logic based on Godel algebras and their embeddings in relational structures, specifically focusing on relativized modal logic and hybrid logic systems. Initially, we outline Godel algebras and algebras with operators derived from them, followed by investigations into epistemic modal logic within these frameworks. Notably, we demonstrate how to interpret modal logic at finite levels within Godel algebras and their operator extensions by applying the Lebesgue measure function. Moreover, we establish equivalence between certain relational structures and Godel algebras, including their operator extensions, which enables the application of Henkin's theorem to determine characterizations for relational structures through algebras. Furthermore, we explore how to extend the epistemic modal logic system to accommodate additional axioms and the distribution property. Additionally, we analyze hybrid logic based on Godel algebras, specifically focusing on the expression of modal operators using preconditions. Lastly, all results are generalized to algebras with operators for both Sahlqvist and Godel modal logics. All in all, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of Godel modal logic and its extensions by examining its representations in relational structures and algebras. Nonetheless, many-open world semantics for these logic systems remain an unresolved issue. This research is an extension of earlier work on algebras derived from posets and their applications in modal logic under preclusion. By examining the underlying combinatorial structure of these systems, we establish a range of recursive formulas that enable efficient computation of their thermodynamic parameters, extending a similar result previously obtained for planar graphs. Specifically, we derive one-step recurrences for the partition function, magnetization, and second-moment, which collectively provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing these systems. This framework includes an algorithm for determining the connectivity of graph components, which can be applied to explore the parameter space of these random fields. As a result, we show that these systems exhibit a continuous phase transition if, and only if, their parameters lie within a region that can be precisely defined. This region is characterized by a specific, computable subset of the graph's path-connected components. Finally, we outline a corresponding extension of these methods to random fields based on trees. This work offers a novel, graph-theoretic perspective on the thermodynamics of these systems and provides a foundation for exploring its dynamics. Additionally, it facilitates the development of more efficient approximation methods, such as loop series, and may also be adapted to systems with non-uniform node weights. In neural machine translation, the target sentence is generated sequence by sequence, with each target word built upon the previous word. Previous studies have shown that neural machine translation models can leverage look-ahead information to enhance the current target word prediction. This paper proposes a novel look-forward attention mechanism that allows the model to focus on target words further down the sequence on each translation step. By integrating this mechanism into a layer-by-layer attention network, we achieve significant improvements in BLEU scores across various language pairs and find that the proposed model's performance closely matches that of state-of-the-art transformer models. Notably, our results indicate that the look-forward attention mechanism is particularly beneficial for less-frequent words, contributing substantially to the overall gain. Moreover, we discover that the proposed model's ability to focus on distant target words is crucial for better handling of long sentences, and that look-forward attention can complement existing neural machine translation techniques, such as sentence-level attention and hierarchical architectures. Overall, our work provides a compelling case for the broader application of look-forward attention in neural machine translation. The proposed model's implementation is also adaptable to multi-stage generation models, such as models using the hierarchical recurrent neural network, and we anticipate that our work will inspire the exploration of more complex attention models in neural machine translation. As data becomes increasingly complex and numerous in both quality and quantity, researchers face significant challenges in their analysis. This is particularly true for Gaussian random field models, which are commonly used but can be computationally expensive to implement, especially when dealing with large datasets. To address these limitations, we present an alternative approach based on Mat\'ern Gaussian models that leverages sparsity in graphs. Our method employs a nonstationary Mat\'ern Gaussian process prior on the graph, which is then integrated with convex optimization techniques to efficiently estimate model parameters. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through numerous experiments, showcasing its advantage in both model complexity and computational efficiency compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we apply our model to real-world datasets in both classification and regression tasks, achieving superior performance. Our code is openly available for reproducibility purposes. This approach offers substantial improvements in computational performance without compromising too much accuracy, making it particularly suitable for larger datasets. In such cases, our method outperforms previous approaches by an order of magnitude in terms of computational cost while incurring only a relatively small increase in model complexity. This efficient Mat\'ern Gaussian process model also facilitates Conjugate Gradient-based optimization, leading to significant improvements in efficiency. In addition, we uncover a connection between our model and Neumann series, which enables us to model nonstationarity by aggregating multiple stationary components, each with distinct scales. The creation of efficient urban road mapping relies on a variety of data sources, including satellite imagery, GPS signals from smartphones, and vehicle movement tracking. This research focuses on extracting urban road information by analyzing the navigation patterns of a large number of vehicles in a given area, utilizing their collective journey data. This approach is particularly relevant for regions lacking detailed road maps, such as some urban areas in developing countries or cities with frequently changing road layouts. To address this challenge, this paper develops an unsupervised, clustering-based algorithm to identify the most frequently traveled road networks by grouping journey data based on similarity. To counter noise in data and prevent no-route indications from skewing results, this research involves journey pairs that have matched beginnings and ends but failed to detect a road connection. With the help of simulated and real-world data, including ride-hailing vehicle journey logs in Shanghai, this research demonstrates its efficient performance and data resilience capabilities. Furthermore, this method's efficiency makes it an adaptable solution for urban road detection across various regions. This research was published in IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems in 2018. This work has since been expanded into a new clustering algorithm and validated with ride-hailing vehicle data in Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen, with a corresponding update to the original paper also being submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems for review. This updated research explores the effects of varying data quantity, quality, and quality on urban road network detection, in addition to providing a preliminary analysis of extracted network topological characteristics in comparison to actual mapping data. A blockchain-based smart contract network, Tezos, employs a formal approach to create and assess smart contracts. This process involves two phases: initial assessment by Tezos nodes and later verification of contracts through a commander-in-chief node. Our research focuses on enhancing the second verification phase by introducing a novel validation tool, HELMHOLTZ, tailored for Tezos smart contracts expressed in Michelson using Quotient Types and Refinement Types. By leveraging the refinement types, developers can mark valid Michelson expressions, thereby allowing HELMHOLTZ to efficiently identify genuine refinements from suspected ones with a type-checking time of approximately 10 microseconds on average. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of HELMHOLTZ by applying our method to a notable smart contract and comparing its performance with the existing Tezos implementation. Furthermore, we explore potential security benefits and a notable reduction in assessment time by incorporating Refinement Types, an area we plan to explore further in upcoming research. We thoroughly evaluate our approach using real-world datasets from multiple domains, and our code is publicly available for reproducibility. Our findings not only enhance understanding of GCNNs but also provide a framework for a comprehensive analysis of neural network components. Furthermore, our work showcases the versatility of matched filtering in uncovering the inner workings of complex neural network modules. In the context of data analytics, our approach serves as a valuable resource for identifying the underlying mathematical concepts that relate neural network performance to data characteristics. In the process, we also provide a method for evaluating the robustness of neural network interpretations. This research paper examines local approximation techniques for local solutions to specific PDE equations, including the porous medium equation and the rapid diffusion equation, within a broad, non-compact metric measure space environment that has a compact boundary. Existing works primarily focused on narrow, homogeneous domains, whereas this study relaxes those restrictions, instead exploring approximation methods that rely on a linear combination of the gradient and the distance to the boundary. Key properties, including existence, uniqueness, and boundary behavior, are proven for a broad class of superlinear equations, as well as their nonlinear counterparts, through a combination of approximation techniques, fixed point theorems, and measure-theoretic inequalities. Additionally, this study proves that solutions to these approximated equations converge to the original equation solutions, demonstrating the benefits of local approximation methods for addressing challenging nonlinear problems. A compactness result is also established for a broad class of rapid diffusion equations, revealing multiple solution branches and confirming the existence of anorbid patterns of a free boundary problem. A related work on a Hele-Shaw type equation is also presented, along with potential applications to a free boundary problem involving a porous medium equation and a Hamiltonian elliptic equation. We examine how Godel's first incompleteness theorem from 1931 has been reinterpreted through the eyes of different logicians, focusing on the perspectives of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. Although all four achieved similar results, their methods differed significantly, revealing varied insights into the nature of first-order arithmetic's incompleteness. Our exploration delves into the historical context surrounding the development of these theorems and the logicians' motivations, as well as the subsequent impact of the results on the epistemic framework advocated by Carnap. Furthermore, we leverage the distinct incompleteness theorems established by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser to gain a deeper understanding of the nature of the incompleteness phenomenon, culminating in a discussion on the implications of these results for the concept of a formalistic account of truth. Ultimately, our study offers a historical framework for the development of the incompleteness theorems and the logicians' interpretations, as well as a critical examination of the philosophical implications of these results within the framework of Carnap's views. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of the achievements of all four logicians within the broader context of the evolution of the incompleteness theorems. Finally, we reflect on the enduring influence of the incompleteness theorems on the development of logic and mathematics, as well as on the practitioners of these disciplines. This paper formulates three spheres theorems for functions subject to certain conditions derived from the Dirac equation in higher dimensional Euclidean space. In particular, we establish three spheres theorems for monogenic functions, tangentially monogenic functions, and harmonic functions in R^n+1. Additionally, we explore connections between these results and the Helmholtz Decomposition Theorem in Clifford analysis. Furthermore, we introduce an alternative approach to proving three spheres theorems and derive a new version of the Helmholtz Decomposition Theorem as a consequence. Finally, we discuss potential applications and future directions for these results within Clifford analysis. In addition to three spheres theorems, we also obtain a new version of Boasson's Theorem and a new version of the extension property for monogenic functions along a surface in R^n+1. These new results are then applied to obtain a new version of the extension property for tangentially monogenic functions along a surface in R^n+1. All theorems and results mentioned in this paper can also be extended to the real n-dimensional space R^n+1 equipped with the Euclidean metric. Notably, we also consider the specific case of R^3+1. All proofs and derivations of the results mentioned in this paper rely on the use of spheres with varying radii. Specifically, we employ (k-1)-spheres with radius k, for k equal to 2, 3, and so on, throughout our proofs and derivations. It is essential to the results presented in this paper that the radii of these spheres are distinct. In solving inverse problems, finding a probability distribution associated with partial measurements is crucial. However, current deep learning methods for image inverse problems, such as Computed Tomography reconstruction and phase retrieval, often focus directly on reconstructing the original image, making it difficult to model the underlying probability distribution of images and measurements. To address this limitation, a new framework is proposed that extracts the conditional distribution of images given measurements using a regularized conditional GAN, obtained from a regularized mini-batch conditional Wasserstein GAN. To minimize the complexity of optimizing multiple GANs, a shared latent space is introduced and regularized mini-batch conditional cross entropy is proposed to achieve this efficiency. Furthermore, a mini-batch energy-based model is suggested to investigate whether the proposed framework can effectively capture the underlying probability distribution of images and measurements, leading to the development of a new algorithm that combines a regularized conditional GAN and a mini-batch energy-based model. Experimental evaluations show that the proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art deep learning methods in multiple applications, including CT reconstruction, phase retrieval, and deblurring. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhkqkq/RCGAN. Leveraging the proposed framework, a novel method is also introduced for solving general inverse problems with non-blind cases, outperforming existing approaches. Additionally, the paper provides an early exploration of the framework's potential applications to super-resolution and blind deconvolution issues. Furthermore, the issue of whether the proposed framework can effectively solve blind deconvolution problems is raised for future research. Future work will concentrate on enhancing the proposed framework's performance for specific tasks through task-specific modifications and exploring its potential as a general framework for solving various inverse problems. The paper introduces a new evaluation metric called structural blur-specific metric for assessing the quality of deblurred images, providing a preliminary examination of the framework's potential applications to low-light image enhancement, demosaicing, and despeckling images. The paper contains novel theoretical insights on the convergence and regularization capabilities of the proposed algorithm, including a new analysis on the effect of adding noise to measurements, as well as scenarios where the proposed framework successfully captures the underlying probability distribution of images and measurements. The paper is co-cited by the journal paper listed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04114, and the issue of whether the proposed framework can effectively capture the underlying probability distribution of images and measurements in underdetermined cases, such as compressive sensing, is raised for future research. This article examines the existence of invariant surfaces in fractional-order dynamical systems that are defined by specific polynomial equations. We provide a comprehensive test for determining whether invariant surfaces exist at a particular location, and we demonstrate its utility by investigating the stability of invariant surfaces in various fractional-order systems, such as the Rossler, Clegg, and Murali-lakshmi systems. Our analysis reveals that certain of these systems have invariant surfaces only under very strict conditions, whereas others do not have invariant surfaces under any circumstances. We also establish that some of these systems can exhibit chaotic behavior despite not having invariant surfaces. We conclude that our test is a crucial tool for evaluating the stability of invariant surfaces, and we propose it as a means for identifying new fractional-order dynamic systems that do not have invariant surfaces. We make our test publicly available through an online application. Additionally, we provide a nonexistence criterion for invariant volumes in the presence of full rank Lie brackets. This criterion allows us to prove that certain fractional Clegg systems do not have invariant volumes. We also consider the problem of controlling the location of invariant surfaces and volumes using global stabilization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the Murali-lakshmi system, for which it yields a novel invariant surface at a desired location. We discuss several potential extensions and generalizations of our results. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations and provide a discussion of the implications of our results for the behavior of fractional-order dynamical systems. We conclude that our results open up new directions for the study of fractional-order dynamical systems and that further research in this area is warranted. To overcome these difficulties, our proposed system utilizes a limited number of rapid, low-accuracy training iterations to identify the best multi-hop pairings, followed by more precise beam training in each link. To optimize this two-stage process, we develop a method that first identifies the optimal coarse training selections through a grid search, after which it applies reinforcement learning to refine the beam training process in each link, resulting in improved spectral efficiency. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed system, yielding a 50% improvement in spectral efficiency and reduced training time. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the gain in spectral efficiency is linearly correlated with the frequency range. Additionally, we investigate the optimal allocation of training time between the coarse and fine stages, finding that an imbalance can lead to suboptimal performance. To mitigate the load of the central processor, we explore the integration of edge processing capabilities, enabling partial processing and reducing data transfer. Simulation results indicate that this hybrid approach provides a 20% gain in efficiency. Finally, we examine the potential performance gains of our proposed system in realistic scenarios. To do this, we simulate a scenario with 10 base stations serving a total of 50 users, resulting in a 25% improvement in spectral efficiency. Lastly, we investigate the impact of increasing the number of antennas at the central processor on performance, showing that while it leads to greater complexity, it is nonetheless worthwhile. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed system in multi-hop Terahertz communication systems. The ISM's structure can be deduced through the study of pulsar scintillation, which is influenced by ionized clouds in the line of sight between the pulsar and Earth.  By examining the statistical patterns of scintillations in pulsar signals, researchers can gain information about the size and velocity of these clouds.  The detection of similar scintillation patterns in multiple observations of the pulsar B1133+16 from the Parkes radio telescope suggests the presence of large, coherent structures in the ISM over several thousand AU.  The duration of these structures, as determined by the velocity and frequency characteristics, is approximately one hundred thousand kilometers.  The existence of such large structures in the ISM, first hypothesized through the eyes of a pulsar, is consistent with the theoretical framework of magnetized plasmas maintained by the large-scale magnetic field of the Galaxy.  Future research with more sensitive radio telescopes, such as the Square Kilometre Array, will be able to refine this line of inquiry and provide a deeper understanding of the Galaxy's magnetic field and its impact on the ISM.  The method of examining the regional ISM using scintillometry of pulsars is also applicable to a wide range of other pulsars, which will allow for a more comprehensive study of this phenomenon.  The fact that the scintillometry patterns in B1133+16 are consistent across a wide frequency range, spanning from 0.72 to 1.4 GHz, indicates that this structure is not a phenomenon unique to a specific frequency, which in turn implies that this method of research is equally effective across this range.  The study of these structures and their velocity dispersion may also provide a better understanding of the local ISM, which in turn could shed light on the composition and dynamics of the Galaxy's outer regions. To enhance the quality of speech synthesis, significant progress has been made in recent years, largely driven by the success of neural network-based approaches. In particular, WaveNet models have produced high-fidelity speech samples by modeling raw waveforms directly. However, these models face challenges in scaling to longer speech segments due to their extensive computational requirements and memory constraints. Our proposed Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) addresses these limitations by incorporating a novel pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layer that balances low-frequency component capture with reduced parameter count. By leveraging this layer, QPNet achieves comparable quality to traditional WaveNet models while significantly reducing model size and inference time. When trained on 8-kHz speech samples, QPNet demonstrates a significant increase in naturalness, outperforming other compact speech synthesis models. Notably, our results show that a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layer can amply substitute the traditional WaveNet layer, even in the absence of pitch extraction, thereby resulting in a more compact model with improved speech quality. Furthermore, QPNet exhibits great potential for larger-scale datasets, suggesting a promising future for this model architecture in speech synthesis applications. Our findings also validate the utility of dilated convolution layers in modeling quasi-periodic signals through the capture of underlying pattern periods. Ultimately, our open-source implementation of QPNet achieves high-quality speech samples at 8 kHz and 16 kHz sampling rates. In particular, our code is available on GitHub at the specified URL. Our model also won first prize in the 3rd Interspeech Challenge on Highly Variable Speech Synthesis. Furthermore, we explore the integration of QPNet with a speech synthesis system comprising a text-to-speech front-end, which prompts the generation of raw speech waveforms. Our results show that QPNet can generate high-fidelity speech at 8 kHz and 16 kHz sampling rates with a range of speech rates and styles. Our model is particularly effective in producing natural-sounding speech from longer transcriptions. Although it can handle shorter transcriptions, speech from these is often characterized as childlike. Our code can be trained on a range of speech datasets, including those with longer speech segments. However, such datasets necessitate the use of quasi-autoregressive models like QPNet to prevent memory constraints during training. Our model outperforms other compact speech synthesis models in terms of naturalness, as evidenced by high ratings from multiple evaluation metrics, including mean opinion score, frequency-weighted mean opinion score, and frequency-weighted mean absolute error. The standard Arabic script is rich in distinct characters with varying forms, making written Arabic prone to spelling errors in written forms and inconsistent morphological analysis in written inputs. To address these issues, several studies have explored the potential of standardizing the written form of Arabic, either by standardizing the spelling or the morphological analysis. In this research, we introduce a unique approach that combines both objectives and offers a comprehensive solution for both issues. We present the design and functionality of the MADARi platform, an interactive web-based tool allowing users to input standardized forms of Arabic words. The platform leverages multiple resources, including dictionaries and morphological analyzers, to provide consistent morphological analysis, spelling corrections, and part-of-speech tagging for each input word. In addition to standardizing the spelling and morphological analysis, the MADARi platform aims to establish a standardized corpus of Arabic words, making it a valuable resource for natural language processing, lexicography, and language teaching. The platform is publicly accessible at https://madari.seclab.org/. For further information on incorporating the MADARi standard into your research or project, please refer to the guidelines available at the same website. The standardized forms of Arabic words, including those in the corpus, are licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. The MADARi platform is developed using the MEAN stack, with MongoDB, Express.js, Angular.js, and Node.js as its core technologies. The underlying algorithms, as well as the complete source code of the platform, are openly available on the SECLAB GitHub repository at https://github.com/seclab-ku/. Planetary environments can be diverse, consisting of multiple substances including gases, liquids, solids, and various physical states.  The analysis of an exoplanet's spectral data to determine its composition can be complicated by numerous possible elements and their varying absorption patterns.  To tackle this challenge, a method has been developed to break down the analysis into several individual calculations of elemental absorption against known standards, thereby facilitating the identification of elements despite complex atmospheric conditions.  This approach is particularly effective when employing broad-band spectroscopy, and is especially useful for identifying elements like oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen, which are typically present in molecular forms and can only be detected through their absorption of light as these substances are fundamental to the formation of H--O--C molecules.  By applying this method to the study of several temperate exoplanets, their atmospheres were found to contain varying amounts of elements including water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia, and iron oxide, with clouds or volatiles dominating in all but one system; with further analysis indicating that the photochemical reactions caused by the incoming starlight can break down certain molecules into others, as evidenced by the higher concentrations of certain elements near the sections of the planet that are directly exposed to the star.  This process is so potent that even the side of the planet facing the star is not saturated with all available molecular forms, implying that the breaking of larger molecules can occur across the entire planet, with potential be beneficial to the search for life by explaining the formation of necessary organic molecules.  This research also provides a method for assessing the photochemical reactions occurring within these distant atmospheres, and offers several new targets for the study of exoplanetary environments, with the potential to improve the accuracy of future predictions of these systems by using models that account for the breaking of large molecules, as well as the formation of clouds and the effects of volatility on the breakdown of molecules, with the goal of better understanding how these environments give rise to the spectral patterns that can be detected from Earth.  This study proposes multiple follow-up observations, as well as the analysis of existing data using the new approach, with the goal of further exploring the complex atmospheric conditions within temperate exoplanets, with particular emphasis on the interaction between host star light and the planetary environment, with the ultimate goal of gaining a deeper understanding of these systems, with implications for the search for life, and the study of planetary formation and evolution, as well as the potential for the discovery of novel astronomical phenomena. This approach leverages tunneling spectroscopy with Ohmic damping and resistive electrodes to analyze superconducting islands. The proposed technique involves two measurements: first, conducting tunneling spectroscopy with highly conductive electrodes that can discern the Z2 periodicity; second, using electrodes with high resistance to introduce Ohmic damping, effectively obscuring the periodicity, and comparing the outcomes with the first-party data. The rationale behind this method is to address the precision limitations of normal junction tunneling spectroscopy and the contamination issues associated with using highly conductive electrodes in the presence of a strong superconducting source lead. These functors retain key properties of coherent functors, enabling the expansion of Delooping principles to a broader range of situations. This paper delves into the specifics of shadow functors, building on the concepts of coherent functors and Delooping functors. By examining the fundamental characteristics of shadow functors, it becomes possible to generalize the principle of Degeneration Preservation to any functor that can be expressed as a combination of Delooping and coherent functors. This generalized form is then applied to demonstrate the equivalence between homotopy theories characterized by specific properties. Ultimately, this framework is utilized to establish the equivalence between the homotopy theories associated with bicategories that are locally equivalent. This paper also explores the relationship between shadow functors and categories of homotopy coherent diagrams, establishing that such a category can be viewed as the collection of shadow functors from a single bicategory. Finally, this insight is leveraged to prove that the category of homotopy coherent diagrams in a bicategory is equivalent to the homotopy theory of that bicategory. This is then coupled with an observation about the direction of mapping in bicategorical diagrams, enabling the derivation of a related but distinct property, homotopy coherent functors preserving shadows, that serves as a prerequisite for our primary result. This latter property is shown to be a prerequisite for a functor to be homotopy coherent, effectively providing a characterization of homotopy coherent functors in terms of their behavior with respect to bicategorical diagrams. However, real-world data is often inaccurately represented using such simplistic graphs as they fail to capture the temporal aspects and the direction of relationships between entities. For instance, Facebook friendships can be bidirectional but a driver's navigation relies heavily on directed relationships between road intersections and includes temporal aspects. Utilizing Euclidean space embeddings, we introduce LGNN, a novel neural network that operates on directed, temporal-free graphs and incorporates time-based interactions. LGNN outperforms existing GNN models on six benchmark datasets and offers unparalleled performance on three real-world scenarios. Furthermore, LGNN exhibits a 20% decrease in loss for counterfactual events and a 12% increase in future prediction accuracy for datasets with temporal relationships. The proposed extension adds vectorial operators to the core modal $\mu$-calculus, while maintaining the same safety properties as the original. However, we find that the security aspect is no longer guaranteed with the additional operators when transitioning from a world to a successor world. The resulting complexity ranges from NP to NP-complete for the restricted formulas and generally NP-complete for the full satisfiability within the expanded modal $\mu$-calculus. The only exception is when the signature comprises a single atomic proposition, in which case the complexity is determined by the number of particles. A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs extends to various other graph theoretic constructs, including coverings and homomorphisms. By examining the notion of extended double covers, this paper also investigates the concept of homeomorphically invariant limits of signed graphs. These homeomorphically invariant limits are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence with specific classes of signed graphs, and we explore the implications of this connection. Furthermore, we establish that the class of graphs that correspond to these limits are equal to the class of 3-degenerate subgraphs, and we also provide a more general result regarding the relationship between homeomorphically invariant limits and homomorphism factors. Additionally, this paper is not without its own contributions to the study of extended double covers, as it demonstrates that the property of being an EDT is neither an intersection nor a union closed class for groups of graphs, and we present general criteria for determining whether a graph has an EDT that is homeomorphic to another specified graph. Furthermore, we identify specific pairs of graphs for which the question of whether an EDT exists between them remains unanswered, and we establish a connection between certain 2-factorizations and EDTs in certain triply connected graphs. This research on EDTs is shown to be related to the study of homeomorphically invariant limits of signed graphs, and we explore how the property of being an EDT is inherited when moving to a graph that is homeomorphic to the original graph. Lastly, we apply and extend several previously reported results on coverings, homomorphisms, and homeomorphically invariant limits of signed graphs, and we present solutions to certain specific open questions and problems presented in prior research. For instance, we demonstrate that the graph $C_5$ has an EDT that is homeomorphic to $K_2$, and we show that the smallest number of edges in an EDT for the graph $K_m$ is equal to $\frac{m^2+m}{2}$ when $m$ is an odd number greater than 3. Additionally, we present an EDT for the graph $T_6$ that consists of 12 edges, and we demonstrate that the graph $K_{3,3,1}$ has an EDT that is homeomorphic to the complete graph $K_5$. Lastly, we conclude by outlining several directions for further research on the topics of extended double covers, homomorphisms, and homeomorphically invariant limits of signed graphs.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histology is crucial to determine the risk of cancer, as some polyps can transform into malignant tumors if left untreated. The process of analyzing these samples involves histological examination by a pathologist, who assesses their appearance to make a diagnosis. However, this method is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and subject to human error. To bridge the gap between human expertise and the efficiency of automated analysis, computer vision techniques can be trained on a large dataset of annotated images. Unfortunately, high-quality datasets of colorectal polyp images are scarce, hindering the development of accurate classification models. To address this issue, our research team acquired a substantial dataset of over 13,000 images, annotated by multiple pathologists to identify areas of normal tissue, hyperplasia, intraepithelial neoplasia, and invasive carcinoma, as well as mark regions of interest such as crypts, borders, and mucosa. To further enhance the dataset's utility, we applied region-based object recognition, incorporating information about the location and characteristics of each region, and obtained outstanding results on a state-of-the-art evaluation metric. The annotated dataset and our experiments provide valuable insights for researchers aiming to enhance the accuracy of their models. The data, which comprises 13,168 whole-slide images, 51,824 histology images, and 517,679 region-of-interest masks, is an extensive resource for researchers working on computer vision tasks, particularly those related to colorectal polyp analysis. The data we collected raises important questions about data diversity, necessitating further research into data annotation strategies that promote diversity without compromising labeling accuracy. The dataset we presented, named UniToPatho, is now available for other researchers to build upon our findings and contribute to the advancement of computer vision technology. The challenging task of evaluating the accuracy of machine learning models for colorectal polyp analysis has been addressed by developing a comprehensive evaluation framework that combines classification and segmentation evaluation metrics. The framework, coupled with the UniToPatho dataset, provides a foundation for further breakthroughs in this field. To facilitate collaboration and knowledge exchange, we open-source our dataset processing pipeline, which is designed to streamline the annotation process and make it more efficient. The UniToPatho dataset is a significant step forward in leveraging computer vision for the analysis of colorectal polyps, and we believe it will pave the way for more effective and accurate diagnostic tools. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in chondrite meteorites from the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk falls. Isotopic measurements of hydrogen, water content, and oxygen isotopes allowed us to determine the isotopic composition of hydrogen in these meteorites. Since hydrogen isotopes can record the temperature at which hydrogen exists as a solid within planetesimals, we found that the measured values above -10°C indicate the presence of hydrogen bound in water molecules within the interior of these small inner solar system bodies. Additionally, we observed a larger water content in Benenitra than in Chelyabinsk, which we suggest could be an indication of varying orbital paths taken by these small inner solar system planetesimals. It is also possible that this discrepancy may be the result of different impact break-apart points on the parent asteroids or diverse accretion formation environments. Our findings are consistent with the idea that moist accretion occurred within the inner solar system and provide a basis for further investigation into how water was delivered to the terrestrial planets. Water delivery to Mars could have been in the form of late accreting planetesimals with high water contents, as supported by the current water composition of Mars, which includes both dry and wet regions on its surface. We address the challenge of accurately simulating light interaction with dielectric materials using different multipolar expansions under various conditions. By comparing different expansions, we demonstrate that to minimize scattering errors, a combination of electric and magnetic dipolar fields is necessary for calculations beyond the long wavelength approximation. Furthermore, we show that for light scattering calculations within the long wavelength approximation, both spherical harmonic and multipolar expansions converge at a similar rate, but beyond this limit, the multipolar expansion converges more slowly. However, we find that both methods can be used to predict the optical properties of materials but may require a higher order expansion for accuracy. We also examine how different expansions relate to each other and demonstrate that they all converge to the same physical properties. As a result, we recommend using the simplest expansion that can accurately predict a material's optical properties to avoid overfitting. We apply these findings to dielectric materials with spatial variations in refractive index across multiple length scales. We propose a new method for simulating light interaction with these materials that prioritizes convergence and accuracy, involving a multi-step process that utilizes expansions tailored to different spatial scales. We validate our approach by predicting the scattering behavior and optical properties of these materials, showing that it yields accurate results that align with experimental observations. This study introduces the concept of quantum immanents for representations associated with Schur algebras, extending a notion from classical immanents. Specifically, we define double Young-Capelli bitableaux and demonstrate their equivalence to products of representations, paralleling the classical Capelli method. From this, we derive altered Schur functions as a combination of these bitableaux, connecting them to plethysm relations. Our findings also link quantum immanents to combinatorial objects, revealing connections through the symmetrizable Cartan matrix and Dynkin diagram, and demonstrating the combinatorial nature of certain Schur algebra results. Finally, we establish relationships between quantum immanents, double Young-Capelli bitableaux and the combinatorial objects known as (p,t)-hook formulas. Our analysis expands upon prior work by J. M. Zeidan in a personal communication. We introduce Swift, a newly developed, open-source Newtonian N-body simulation library for flat domains. Swift is designed to efficiently handle complex particle interactions and boundary collisions within rectangular domains. It achieves this by dividing the boundaries into manageable segments and assigning corresponding collision detection responsibilities to multiple threads. This modular approach enables rapid adaptation to various domain shapes and sizes. Additionally, Swift includes versatile import and export tools for importing external potentials, exporting intermediate data, and integrating with multiple visualization and analysis programs. These features make Swift particularly useful as a pre-processing tool for numerical simulations. We showcase Swift's performance on several challenging scenarios, including simulations of stuck or separating particles, and demonstrate its speed benefits over other leading N-body solvers. Furthermore, we highlight Swift's compatibility with multiple programming languages, its modular code architecture, and its seamless integration with popular scientific computation frameworks.
